items.title: AI pull requests in open source have a context problem
items.summary: Merged pull requests on [GitHub climbed](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/github-gives-maintainers-a-throttle-for-the-ai-pull-request) from 25 million a month in January 2023 to 90 million a month in March 2026, and GitHub ties the jump to agentic workflows. Many of the ones landing in open source queues show up without the context a maintainer needs to accept them, like whether the change follows the project's rules or duplicates a fix someone already sent. Fatih Kadir Akın knows that queue well. He built [prompts.chat](https://prompts.chat), an open prompt library with more than 175,000 GitHub stars, and works as a developer advocate on Automattic's WordPress team. On The Merge, he told Hendrik Krack where the problem sits: > The code itself may be slop, or it can be really nice code. The problem is that whoever is controlling the agent isn't controlling it very well. The missing piece is context. Neither the agent nor the person running it supplies any, so the maintainer has to rebuild it in review. ## What agent-written PRs miss The [prompts.chat repo](https://github.com/f/prompts.chat) keeps a CSV copy of the prompt database, and a worker regenerates that file every day. Hand edits to the CSV vanish within a day, even after Fatih merges them. The PR template and CONTRIBUTING.md both say not to touch it, and agents keep sending PRs that edit it anyway. Fatih puts it plain and simple, “the agents don't care.” AutoGPT hit the same wall. Better contributor guidelines and docs [changed nothing](https://github.blog/open-source/maintainers/your-contributors-are-ai-first-now-is-your-project/), because agents don't go looking for documentation unless something points them to it. Duplicates make it worse. Fatih suspects plenty of contributors just point an agent at the open issues and tell it to send fixes. The result is one bug fixed several times by agents that never checked for an open PR, with the maintainer reading every copy. ## Put the rules where agents will read them Maintainers are answering with rules agents can't miss and limits they can't get around: - **Instructions beside the code** AutoGPT put its rules in AGENTS.md files next to the code they govern and pointed its CLAUDE.md files at them, so any agent working in that directory picks them up. - **A contribution guide for agents** Jesse Vincent wrote one into the CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files for [Superpowers](https://github.com/obra/superpowers), and Hendrik says PRs that ignore it get rejected automatically. - **A written AI policy** Home Assistant's [AI policy](https://contributors.home-assistant.io/blog/2026/07/20/ai-policy/) welcomes AI as an aid and closes any PR or issue an agent opened on its own. Project lead Franck Nijhof [puts it plainly](https://frenck.dev/open-source-was-not-ready-for-ai-speed-contributions/): AI makes contributions cheap to produce, and maintainers still have to verify every one. - **Limits on the queue** GitHub now lets maintainers [restrict PRs to collaborators or cap how many](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/github-gives-maintainers-a-throttle-for-the-ai-pull-request) a user without write access can have open. Fatih plans to dig into how Superpowers handles it for prompts.chat. He calls the current moment chaos, but he's betting agents get better at following a project's rules as the models improve. ![Contribution instructions and code sit together in an open project folder, linked by orange arrows.](/content/assets/the-merge-fatih/rules-beside-code.webp) ## The maintainer still approves the merge Rules don't change who signs off. CodeRabbit reviews every prompts.chat PR first and does most of the hard work, and Copilot sometimes takes a second pass. Fatih still reads the code before anything merges. "The biggest problem is that you have to be an approver as a human. I'm merging it to something that works on the internet. I should be careful." That last read is exhausting even at prompts.chat's volume, and bigger projects get far more. OpenCode was pulling in around 200 new PRs a day when [Ryan Vogel came on The Merge](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/the-merge-ryan-vogel-deciding-what-to-keep). Daniel Stenberg, who maintains curl and has [written about AI-generated reports](https://daniel.haxx.se/blog/2026/10/22/ignore-the-slop/) for years, says the project can't just ignore them, because some of them find real flaws. The volume costs goodwill too. During one rush, Fatih closed PRs without a comment, and he worries that silent closes can come off as rude. ## Context is the contributor's job Fatih's advice goes to the other side of the PR. Asked what developers should learn now, he went straight to communication. People used to ask how he got ChatGPT to do what he wanted, and his answer was that he's a communicator first, someone who gives talks across Turkey and now in the US. > At the end, you are communicating with the AI agent. You should give context, and context is about communication. A message with no context lands badly with a colleague, and agents react the same way. When friends tell him AI couldn't build their app, he can usually get it working by explaining the problem properly. An open source contribution needs that skill twice: the agent needs the project's context to write a change that fits, and the maintainer needs the contributor's context to trust it. Open source contributors keep landing in the same place, where a contribution counts for more once the person behind it has shown up in the community. That's how it worked for Fatih. He's largely self-taught, and GitHub was where strangers read his code and told him what was wrong with it. Some became contributors, and he still calls it "magical" that someone on the other side of the world will help you build something. ## Verification is the skill to build Fatih trusts coding models more than he used to. Early agents needed him to check every line, and now he thinks they write better code than he does, so his time goes to architecture. "I don't want to be the smartest guy in the room. I just want to build something that works." That trust has limits. One model recently started writing Ruby in the middle of his JavaScript project and went hunting for Ruby files that didn't exist. Verification is the second skill he'd tell new developers to build, and it doesn't depend on writing the language yourself. Fatih has built iOS apps without knowing Swift, and he can still tell when Swift code is wrong. Knowing what a memory leak is lets you point an agent at one when an app keeps crashing. Without that, all you see is the crash. [Kunal Kushwaha made the same case](https://www.coderabbit.ai/blog/software-engineering-skills-ai-kunal-kushwaha): fundamentals are how engineers check what AI tools produce. ![A hand holds a magnifying glass over the connection between a code change and the software modules it affects.](/content/assets/the-merge-fatih/human-verification.webp) Fatih isn't sure where that instinct came from, and practice is the best guess. He used to read other people's code just to see how it was built, including the entire jQuery source. Anyone running an agent against someone else's project needs the same habit, because reading the change is how you find out whether it's worth a maintainer's time. ## Watch the full conversation The episode also gets into how Fatih landed the single-letter GitHub username `f`, and how prompts.chat grew from one README into an app that still credits its contributors on GitHub. Watch the full episode of The Merge. CodeRabbit takes the first pass on every prompts.chat PR, so Fatih's own read starts after the hard work is done. It's [free for open source projects](https://www.coderabbit.ai/faq), and any maintainer fielding agent-written PRs can run the same setup. [Get started with CodeRabbit](https://app.coderabbit.ai/login?free-trial=).

items.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness adds Strands harness defaults, built-in tools, and lifecycle hooks
items.summary: When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund. We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop. With this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints. There’s no new resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use. Strands capabilities, on AWS Strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself. You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability. AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment. A more capable managed harness Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults: A current recommended model. When you omit the model, Harness uses a recommended default model that evolves as new models are released, always keeping your harnesses up to date. Explicit harness-level and per-invocation model configurations continue to take precedence. Task-oriented instructions. The managed system prompt encourages the agent to gather relevant context, use appropriate tools, continue until the task is resolved, adapt to failures or denied actions, and verify its work before reporting completion. The default system prompt improves over time to support the latest harness behavior. Automatic prompt caching. For supported models using Converse on Amazon Bedrock, Harness caches the system prompt, tool definitions, and conversation history. Repeated calls with the same prompt and tool surface can use lower-priced cache-read tokens, reducing input processing latency and cost. Proactive context management. By default, Harness summarizes older conversation turns while retaining recent context once the context window reaches a configurable threshold. Keeping the context lean this way helps Harness run at about 34% lower token cost than other leading harnesses. Context offloading. Large tool results can be moved out of the immediate model context. The agent receives a preview and can retrieve the complete result when needed, reducing repeated context usage without losing access to the data. Planning across invocations. The todo_write tool maintains a structured task plan that can be restored in later invocations within the same session, including after conversation summarization. Focused delegation. The subagent tool delegates a self-contained task to a fresh worker and returns the result to the parent agent. The worker is internal to the invocation, not a separately managed harness resource, and shares invocation limits and your tool-call lifecycle hooks. Web retrieval. The web_fetch tool retrieves content from a specified webpage to give your harness up-to-date external context. Granular filesystem access. With separate read, write, and edit tools, you can grant only the granular filesystem capabilities an agent needs. Customer-provided Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Browser, Code Interpreter, inline functions, skills, memory, and customer-provided containers continue to work through the existing harness interfaces. Recommended by default, configurable when needed Harness manages its defaults so that agents using them receive the current AgentCore recommended experience as models, instructions, context management, and built-in capabilities improve. Explicit configuration always takes precedence: Configure a model ID to keep using a specific model. Configure systemPrompt to completely replace the managed system prompt. Configure truncation to keep a specific context-management policy. List individual allowedTools selectors to maintain a fixed tool surface. When allowedTools is omitted or set to ["*"], Harness provides the current recommended built-in tool set. Because this set can gain capabilities over time, applications with a fixed security or capability boundary should list only the tools they need. For example, the following configuration permits read-only filesystem access and web retrieval without granting shell access or file modification: { "allowedTools": [ "read", "web_fetch" ] } Govern consequential actions with lifecycle hooks With lifecycle hooks, you can run your own deterministic code at defined points in the agent loop. For example, an AWS Lambda function can allow or deny a request or a tool call, and an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic or Amazon EventBridge event bus can receive a notification to record activity or start an asynchronous workflow. Harness supports four lifecycle events: Event When it runs Effect of a Lambda denial before_invocation Before the agent processes the request Stops the invocation with hook_stopped before_tool_call After the model proposes a tool call and before execution Skips the tool call. The agent loop continues after_tool_call After a tool result exists Retains the result and stops before further inference after_invocation After the invocation completes Reports the decision. Output already streamed cannot be retracted Only Lambda hooks can change the agent loop. They run synchronously and return allow or deny, with an optional reason. SNS and Amazon EventBridge hooks are notifications and don’t block the agent loop. For example, a customer-support agent can investigate an order on its own while a before_tool_call hook checks each refund against an approval limit before the refund tool runs. The following configuration attaches that Lambda function to the harness: [ { "beforeToolCall": { "name": "refund_policy", "target": { "lambda": { "arn": "arn:aws:lambda:us-west-2:123456789012:function:refund-policy", "timeoutSeconds": 10, "failureMode": "deny" } } } } ] The function receives the proposed tool call in the hook payload and returns a decision: def lambda_handler(event, _context): tool = event["context"] if tool["toolName"] == "issue_refund" and tool["toolInput"]["amount"] > 500: return {"decision": "deny", "reason": "Refund exceeds the $500 auto-approval limit."} return {"decision": "allow"} When the function denies the call, the harness skips the refund and the agent continues, so it can tell the customer that the request was escalated. Each decision also appears in the InvokeHarness response stream as a hookEvent: { "hookEvent": { "name": "refund_policy", "type": "before_tool_call", "decision": "deny", "reason": "Refund exceeds the $500 auto-approval limit." } } Hooks also apply to subagents. When the agent delegates a task, each tool call the subagent makes runs through the same beforeToolCall and afterToolCall hooks, so delegation can’t bypass your refund policy. The invocation-level hooks (beforeInvocation, afterInvocation) run once for the whole invocation. You configure hooks with CreateHarness or UpdateHarness. If a Lambda function times out or returns an error, the hook applies its failureMode, which defaults to deny. For timeouts, payload fields, and context limits, see Lifecycle hooks in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide. To see every event and target type working together, try the Refund Desk sample in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. A six-step guided tour shows all four lifecycle events and the AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge targets. It also shows validation of client-supplied inline function results and the difference between failureMode deny and allow. Run a multi-agent research coordinator with the AgentCore CLI Creating a harness takes a single command. You name it and set up the instructions, context policy, and limits you want. This example creates a Research Coordinator: a harness with a task-oriented system prompt and summarization-based truncation. In a single invocation, it runs a researcher, a synthesizer, and a reviewer as subagents and returns one consolidated report. You get multi-agent orchestration and context management without provisioning infrastructure or wiring the delegation yourself. The agentcore harness commands call the harness APIs directly, so you don’t need a CLI project or a deployment step. Install the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with npm: npm install -g @aws/agentcore The CLI uses your default AWS credentials. It has no --profile flag, so set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable if you want a specific profile. Save the coordinator’s instructions from the sample as system_prompt.md in your working directory. Create the harness This command passes the coordinator’s system prompt, a summarization policy that keeps the 30 most recent messages intact as the conversation grows, and limits high enough for the full workflow. Because it omits the model, memory, and execution role, the harness uses the current AgentCore recommended model and managed memory, and the CLI creates an execution role in IAM for you. HARNESS_ID=$(agentcore harness create --region us-west-2 --json \ --name ResearchCoordinator \ --system-prompt "$(cat system_prompt.md)" \ --truncation '{"strategy":"summarization","config":{"summarization":{"summaryRatio":0.3,"preserveRecentMessages":30}}}' \ --max-iterations 100 \ --timeout-seconds 3600 \ | jq -r '.harness.harnessId') Creation is asynchronous. Wait for creation to finish. The last command should print READY: while [ "$(agentcore harness get --region us-west-2 --id "$HARNESS_ID" --json | jq -r '.harness.status')" = CREATING ]; do sleep 10; done agentcore harness get --region us-west-2 --id "$HARNESS_ID" --json | jq -r '.harness.status' Send the prompts Invoke your harness with a new session ID. Start with a basic question. The coordinator answers it directly, without calling its subagents: SESSION_ID=$(uuidgen) agentcore harness invoke --region us-west-2 \ --id "$HARNESS_ID" \ --session-id "$SESSION_ID" \ --prompt "What is the current trending topic in AI?" Then ask for a full research report in the same session. The coordinator plans the work and delegates to the researcher, synthesizer, and reviewer in order. It runs at most one revision cycle if the reviewer asks for it, and delivers the final report. Reusing the session ID continues the conversation in the same environment. agentcore harness invoke --region us-west-2 \ --id "$HARNESS_ID" \ --session-id "$SESSION_ID" \ --prompt "Perform a full research report on how data shapes innovations in the tech industry. Use specialized subagents to complete this task. In the final output, clearly state which part each subagent was responsible for, followed by their specific findings." With --prompt, the CLI prints the completed transcript as JSON when the turn finishes. The research run takes about 10 to 15 minutes. To follow along as it works, leave out --prompt, and the CLI opens an interactive chat. The same example in Python (boto3), including the full system prompt, is available in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. Clean up Delete the harness when you’re done. This also deletes its managed memory unless you pass --delete-managed-memory false. The execution role that the CLI created stays in your account, so delete it in the IAM console if you no longer need it. agentcore harness delete --region us-west-2 --id "$HARNESS_ID" Rollout and compatibility On November 11, AgentCore harness began rolling out the Strands harness-backed experience to new and existing harnesses. No customer action is required. Configuration you explicitly provide remains unchanged. Harnesses that omit the model, system prompt, or truncation configuration, or use allowedTools: ["*"], receive the upgraded managed defaults. If your application requires fixed behavior or a fixed capability boundary, configure those settings explicitly. Learn more Create and invoke an AgentCore harness as you do today. Use the managed defaults for the complete current recommended experience, or configure individual settings when your application requires fixed behavior. Strands harness announcement. Get started with AgentCore harness. Managed system prompt. AgentCore harness API reference. Lifecycle hooks. Refund Desk lifecycle hooks code sample. We look forward to seeing what you build with the upgraded AgentCore harness. About the authors Evandro Franco Evandro is a Sr. Data Scientist working on Amazon Web Services. He is part of the Global GTM team that helps AWS customers overcome business challenges related to AI/ML on top of AWS, mainly on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Strands Agents. He has more than 18 years of experience working with technology, from software development, infrastructure, serverless, to machine learning. In his free time, Evandro enjoys playing with his son, mainly building some funny Lego bricks. Diego Brasil Diego is a Domain Specialist Engineer for Generative AI at Amazon Web Services, based in Dublin, Ireland. He helps AWS customers take AI agents from prototype to production, mainly on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Strands Agents, and Kiro. He has more than 13 years of experience in technology. He started in software development and system integration for capital markets platforms at banks and exchanges such as HSBC and B3 (Brazil Stock Exchange and Over-the-Counter Market), then moved into cloud and generative AI. Diego holds an MBA in Digital Business and Artificial Intelligence from USP/ESALQ. Eshan Kumar Eshan is a Software Engineer at Amazon Web Services, based in New York. He works on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and is part of the team that built the AgentCore managed agent harness. His career started in bioengineering, which he studied at UCLA, and he worked as a scientist at Codexis before moving into software and AI. He also studied at Columbia University. Outside of work, Eshan has volunteered with Free The Children and helped build a school for a village in Nicaragua. Amir Hegazy Amir is a Software Engineer at Amazon Web Services, based in New York. He works on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and is part of the team that built the AgentCore managed agent harness. Before AgentCore, he worked on the Amazon Bedrock Converse API, building new features and bringing Anthropic’s Claude models to Converse at launch. He holds a bachelor’s degree in computer science from the University of Southern California. Outside of work, Amir enjoys playing basketball and following Formula 1.

items.title: Amazon Polly launches voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand
items.summary: Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of audio recordings from a speaker who has agreed to have their voice cloned, and Amazon Polly builds your own cloned voice in that speaker’s voice. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning launches with seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region. Access is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. Others can reach out to their AWS account team or apply for access to get access. With this new feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications. Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis, see Amazon Polly Pricing page for details. Hear it for yourself Press play: the first few seconds are a real recording of the speaker, and then their cloned voice takes over with words they never recorded. From recordings to TTS voice. A few minutes of our science lead Trevor’s source audio, and the resulting generative voice. Recorded: “Hello, I’m Trevor, from Science.” Cloned voice: “That first sentence was my real voice. This is my cloned voice, created from a few minutes of my recordings. It can read any text you give it.” Supports seven languages. Hear Jonas, one of the authors, speaking German in his recording and then in his cloned voice: Recorded: “Hallo, ich bin Jonas. Das ist meine echte Stimme.” (Hi, I’m Jonas. This is my real voice.) Cloned voice: “Und das ist meine geklonte Stimme! Gleiche Stimme, neue Worte: Diesen Satz habe ich geschrieben, aber nie aufgenommen.” (And this is my cloned voice! Same voice, new words: I wrote this sentence, but never recorded it.) Use in a variety of applications. Here’s Trevor in a new job he hasn’t had: a non-player character in a game. “Who’s that crossing my bridge? Oh, it’s you again. Same deal as last time: answer my riddle, or hand over the sandwich.” Expand your voice library with voice cloning. Hear this audio sample from AWS Chief Evangelist Jeff Barr: a real recording, then his cloned voice. Recorded: “Hi, I’m Jeff, and this is how I really sound.” Cloned voice: “And this is how my cloned voice sounds, reading a sentence I never recorded.” Hannah: a real recording, then her cloned voice on a support line. Recorded: “Hello, I’m Hannah. This is my real voice.” Cloned voice: “Thanks for calling AnyCompany. Your order 4471 9902 ships today and should arrive on Thursday between 9 AM and 1 PM. Your confirmation code is K-7-Q-2-X-9.” Joely: a real recording, then her cloned voice narrating a lesson. Recorded: “Hi, I’m Joely, and this is how I really sound.” Cloned voice: “In this module, we’ll look at how a neural network learns. First, it makes a guess. Then it measures how far off that guess was, and adjusts, a little at a time.” What you can build A consistent brand voice across channels Establish one recognizable voice and use it across your interactive voice response (IVR) system, cascaded voice agents, mobile app, in-store announcements, advertising, and connected devices. Rather than relying on a generic stock voice or re-booking a recording session each time a script changes, you can generate on-brand audio on demand, with a consistent sound in every channel. Contact centers Deliver a distinctive, on-brand voice across self-service flows, and update prompts as offers and policies change without a new studio session. You can create prompts from source text, test them before rollout, and use the same voice across greeting, routing, and notification experiences. Media and content at scale Creators, publishers, and studios can create audiobooks, courses, podcasts, game characters, and videos in multiple custom voices to enhance the listening experience, and produce subsequent chapters or updates quickly. Localization with a consistent persona Maintain a recognizable voice identity across a content library, so narration remains coherent across titles and updates. Each cloned voice speaks only the language it was recorded in. For multilingual experiences, create and review approved voices per supported language. Accessibility and personalization Offer a natural, human-sounding voice for reading experiences, assistive tools, and personalized interactions. You confirm the speaker’s consent each time you create a voice. How voice cloning works With voice cloning, you can build a custom Amazon Polly voice from recordings of a single speaker and then synthesize speech in that voice through the Amazon Polly generative engine. The voice moves through four steps, from recording the speaker to using the finished voice: Figure 1: The voice cloning lifecycle, from recording a speaker to using the finished voice A cloned voice goes through four steps: Record. You record one speaker (see the following recording tips). You can send the recordings directly in the CreateVoice request or upload them on the console. You can also store them in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the AWS Region where you want the voice and point Amazon Polly to them. Create. You call CreateVoice with 1-10 recordings, the language they are spoken in, and TermsAccepted=True, your confirmation that you have the speaker’s consent. Amazon Polly returns a voice ID (vc-…) right away and builds the voice in the background. Wait. Creation is asynchronous and typically takes 5-10 minutes. During that time, Amazon Polly also checks the quality of your text-to-speech (TTS) voice for speaker similarity. You call GetVoice until the status changes from pending to active or failed. Use. You pass the voice ID to SynthesizeSpeech for real-time audio or to StartSpeechSynthesisTask for long-form audio written to S3, with Engine="generative", the same way you call the other generative voices in Amazon Polly. When you no longer need the voice, you call DeleteVoice. Consent and control A cloned voice is made from one person’s recordings. You confirm that you have the speaker’s consent for all recordings and that you control who can use the voice and when it’s deleted. You confirm consent for each voice you create. When you create a voice, on the console or with TermsAccepted=True in the API, you confirm that you have obtained all rights and consents necessary to create and use the cloned voice. Your use of voice cloning is subject to the AWS Service Terms, the Biometric Notice and Consent Terms, the AWS Responsible AI Policy, and the AWS Acceptable Use Policy. Generated speech carries a watermark. Amazon Polly adds a watermark to text-to-speech audio generated with the cloned voice. Only your account can use it. A cloned voice is scoped to the AWS account that created it, and you control access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). You can encrypt voices with your own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and tag them. You decide when it goes away. Delete a voice with one DeleteVoice call or on the console, once it’s active or its creation has failed. Amazon Polly does not retain a copy of your voice recordings once the voice is created and doesn’t use them to train Amazon Polly models. It keeps only the voice data it needs to synthesize speech, and stores it encrypted. You can use your own AWS KMS key for that encryption, and DeleteVoice removes the data immediately. We recommend that you: Keep a record of each speaker’s consent. Delete the voice if the speaker withdraws consent. Tell listeners when they’re hearing a synthetic voice where that’s appropriate. Grant voice permissions only to the people and systems that need them. For details on intended uses and limitations, see the Amazon Polly AI Service Card and the AWS Responsible Use of AI guidance. Best practices for recordings Your cloned voice learns from the recording, including the parts you’d rather it didn’t: the laptop fan, the room echo, the meeting app’s noise filter. Record two to ten minutes of natural speech, split into takes of up to a minute. You can send up to 10 recordings per voice, and up to 15 minutes of audio in total. Quality matters more than length: more audio might not change how the voice sounds. One speaker, a quiet room, the same distance from the mic. Use a USB microphone, or a phone app that can record WAV. Record in mono WAV, 16-bit, at 24 kHz from the start, so there’s nothing to convert later. Amazon Polly accepts other audio formats, but we recommend WAV. See the Amazon Polly Developer Guide for supported formats and limits. Avoid using meeting apps and browser recorders. Their echo cancellation and noise suppression change the voice, and the clone learns those changes too. Record every take in the style you want the voice to have. The cloned voice takes its style from the recordings and can’t blend several, so upbeat, sad, and angry takes won’t give you a voice that can do all three. Record in the language the voice should speak. Voice cloning is tested with recordings in US English, German, US Spanish, French, Italian, Brazilian Portuguese, and Hindi. Recordings in other accents of these languages, such as British English or Canadian French, also work but are less tested, so check the voice with your own content. Getting started On the console: once voice cloning is enabled for your account (see Availability), expand the left panel and choose Voice cloning, upload up to 10 recordings or select them from Amazon S3, confirm the terms, and choose Create. Each upload can be up to 5 MB. When the voice is ready, try it out on its details page. In code, you need: The latest version of boto3 (pip install --upgrade boto3). IAM permissions for polly:CreateVoice, polly:GetVoice, polly:DescribeVoices, polly:SynthesizeSpeech and polly:DeleteVoice. For long-form audio, also polly:StartSpeechSynthesisTask, polly:GetSpeechSynthesisTask and s3:PutObject on the output bucket. For the following Amazon S3 example: your recordings in a bucket in the Region where you create the voice, with s3:GetObject permission for the IAM role or user that calls CreateVoice. import time import boto3 # Use the Region of your S3 recordings. polly = boto3.client("polly", region_name="us-east-1") # 1. Create a voice from recordings of a speaker who has given consent. # Use 1-10 clean WAV takes of up to a minute each. takes = [ "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/brand-voice/take-1.wav", "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/brand-voice/take-2.wav", "s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket/brand-voice/take-3.wav", ] voice = polly.create_voice( Name="MyBrandVoice", # letters, digits, - and _, up to 64 characters LanguageCode="en-US", # the language spoken in the recordings TermsAccepted=True, # you confirm the speaker's consent and the terms of use VoiceCreationData={ "Recordings": [{"Format": "wav", "Data": {"S3Url": url}} for url in takes], }, Tags={"consent-record": "speaker-0042"}, # optional: the ID of your own consent record, e.g. a signed release # Optional: encrypt the voice with your own KMS key (symmetric, same Region). # Callers who create or use the voice need kms:DescribeKey, # kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt on the key. # CustomerManagedEncryption={ # "KmsKeyArn": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111122223333:key/EXAMPLE" # }, )["Voice"] voice_id = voice["Id"] # for example "vc-0123456789" # 2. Check the status every 30 seconds until the voice is active or failed # (usually a few minutes). Stop with an error after 20 minutes. deadline = time.monotonic() + 20 * 60 while voice["Status"] not in ("active", "failed"): if time.monotonic() > deadline: raise TimeoutError(f"{voice_id} is still {voice['Status']}") time.sleep(30) voice = polly.get_voice(VoiceId=voice_id)["Voice"] if voice["Status"] == "failed": # Check the recordings, delete this voice and create a new one. raise RuntimeError(f"{voice_id}: {voice.get('StatusReason', 'creation failed')}") # 3. Synthesize speech with your new voice. speech = polly.synthesize_speech( VoiceId=voice_id, Engine="generative", LanguageCode="en-US", OutputFormat="mp3", Text="Hello! This is my very own Amazon Polly voice.", ) with open("my-voice.mp3", "wb") as f: f.write(speech["AudioStream"].read()) # When you no longer need the voice: # polly.delete_voice(VoiceId=voice_id) If Python reports that the Polly object has no attribute create_voice, upgrade boto3. For long texts such as audiobook chapters or course modules, use an asynchronous synthesis task that writes the audio to S3: from pathlib import Path task = polly.start_speech_synthesis_task( VoiceId=voice_id, Engine="generative", LanguageCode="en-US", OutputFormat="mp3", OutputS3BucketName="amzn-s3-demo-bucket", OutputS3KeyPrefix="narration/chapter-01", Text=Path("chapter-01.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), # SnsTopicArn="arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:111122223333:polly-tasks", # notify instead of polling )["SynthesisTask"] print(task["TaskId"], task["OutputUri"]) # poll get_speech_synthesis_task until "completed" or "failed" For additional end-to-end Speech AI applications you can build with Amazon Polly, including the voice cloning feature, such as cascaded voice agents and live speech translators, go to the Amazon Polly GitHub repo. Production considerations Create voices ahead of time Voice creation takes minutes, so treat it as a provisioning step, not part of a user request. A small workflow (for example, AWS Step Functions or a job queue) can call CreateVoice, check GetVoice every 30 seconds until the voice is active, and then store the voice ID in your configuration. CreateVoice and DeleteVoice share a limit of 1 request per second, so queue bulk creations and deletions. Keep an inventory DescribeVoices lists your cloned voices alongside the voices built into Amazon Polly. Cloned voices have Origin set to customer. Store the voice ID, Region, language, consent reference, and owner for each voice, and give each voice a unique Name. If a CreateVoice call times out or returns a server error, the voice might already exist, and the SDK’s automatic retries can create a second one. Check DescribeVoices for that name before you try again. Plan for errors CreateVoice returns ThrottlingException when you exceed the 1-request-per-second limit it shares with DeleteVoice, and ServiceQuotaExceededException when the account has reached its cloned-voice quota in that Region. Synthesizing with, or deleting, a voice that is still being created returns ConflictException. If a voice uses your own KMS key, callers without access to the key get an access-denied error. When creation fails, StatusReason gives only a general message, so check the recordings against the preceding recording best practices, then delete the failed voice and create a new one. Scope permissions to voices Cloned voices are IAM resources, so you can give the role that serves traffic permission to synthesize with one voice of choice. If the voice uses your own KMS key, that role also needs access to the key. Keep polly:CreateVoice and polly:DeleteVoice for a separate provisioning role. Here’s an example policy for the serving role: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "polly:SynthesizeSpeech", "Resource": "arn:aws:polly:us-east-1:111122223333:voice/vc-0123456789" } ] } With tags, you can write the same rule once for a whole group of voices using aws:ResourceTag conditions. Review your existing policies too: a statement that allows polly:SynthesizeSpeech on all resources ("Resource": "*") also covers every cloned voice in the account. Plan for quotas and Regions Each account has an initial quota of 10 cloned voices per Region. To request an increase, contact your account team or AWS Support. A voice exists only in the account and Region where you created it. To serve another Region or account, create the voice again in that Region from the same recordings, and make sure the speaker’s consent covers every copy. Test with your real scripts Before a voice goes live, listen to it reading your own content: product names, numbers, addresses, and the longest sentences you have. The same text can come out slightly differently from one request to the next. For fixed prompts such as phone-line greetings, generate the audio once, approve it with the speaker and your brand team, and serve the stored file. If a name or term comes out wrong, spell it differently in the text or use a Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) <phoneme> tag. Phoneme tags work with cloned voices in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish. See Supported SSML tags. Things to know Availability Access is enabled per AWS account. If you see Voice cloning in the Amazon Polly console (expand the left panel and see if Voice cloning is listed), it’s enabled for your account. If not, you can reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to request access. Supported AWS Regions are the same as the generative engine: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Zurich), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). A cloned voice lives in the AWS Region where you created it. Languages English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Tested recording locales: US English (en-US), German (de-DE), US Spanish (es-US), French (fr-FR), Italian (it-IT), Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR), and Hindi (hi-IN). Other accents of these languages also work but are less tested. Each voice speaks the language it was recorded in. Recordings 1-10 recordings per voice, up to 15 minutes in total. WAV is recommended: mono, 16-bit, at 24 kHz or 44.1/48 kHz. Amazon Polly accepts other audio formats too. Console uploads are limited to 5 MB per file. For larger files, use Amazon S3. Data handling Amazon Polly deletes its copy of your recordings once the voice is created and doesn’t use them to train Amazon Polly models. It keeps only the voice data needed for synthesis, stored encrypted (you can use your own AWS KMS key), until you call DeleteVoice. Creation time Typically takes 5-10 minutes to build a TTS voice, asynchronous. Synthesis latency Same as Generative voices in Amazon Polly. Quotas 10 cloned voices per account per AWS Region initially. To request an increase, contact AWS Support. CreateVoice and DeleteVoice share a limit of 1 request per second. Synthesis Cloned voices follow the Amazon Polly quotas for generative voices, including the text limits per request and per synthesis task. See Amazon Polly quotas. Pricing Creating a cloned voice is free. Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis. See Amazon Polly pricing. APIs CreateVoice, GetVoice, DeleteVoice and DescribeVoices to manage voices. SynthesizeSpeech and StartSpeechSynthesisTask with Engine="generative" to use them. See the Amazon Polly API reference. Conclusion Voice cloning in Amazon Polly gives your application a voice people recognize: recorded once, with the speaker’s consent, and ready to use through the Amazon Polly APIs. To get started on the console, make sure Voice cloning is enabled for your account, prepare a recording and the required consent, open the Amazon Polly console, and create your first cloned voice. If you are a new customer and would like to enable voice cloning, reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to get access. For the developer guide, refer to the Amazon Polly documentation. For pricing, see the Amazon Polly Pricing Page. For additional speech AI use cases you can build with Amazon Polly, including voice cloning, check out the GitHub repo. We can’t wait to hear what you build. Thanks to Trevor Wood, Jonas Rohnke, Suyin Wang, Hannah Barrett, Nikie Xiong, Jeff Barr, and Joely Huang for lending us their voices. About the authors Suyin Wang Suyin is a Senior Generative AI Solutions Architect at AWS. She has years of experience building data-driven and machine learning applications that solve real-world problems. She enjoys helping customers identify the right problems to solve and build generative AI solutions that drive business value. In her spare time, she loves singing, or trying out new recipes in the kitchen. Jonas Rohnke Jonas is a Senior Technical Program Manager on Amazon Polly. He brings science, engineering and product together to get new voices from research into customers’ hands, including the cloned voices in this post. He likes plans that stay simple and launches that people actually get to hear. Outside of work, he flies his drone over the English countryside to make short films, and makes chili oil that’s a lot hotter than he admits. Nikie Xiong Nikie is a Senior Technical Product Manager at Amazon Polly. She has 10+ years of experience in AI, voice technology, and bringing innovative products from ideas to launch across consumer and enterprise sectors. With a background in product design and media entertainment production, she thrives at building products and experiences that delight customers. Outside of work, she creates interactive art and enjoys techno.

items.title: Amazon SageMaker AI now detects latency drift, idle GPUs, and missed optimizations on your inference endpoints
items.summary: Every inference endpoint is well tuned the day it goes into production. Teams choose an instance type, serving configuration, and scaling settings that suit the model and its traffic at launch. With the endpoint serving smoothly, they understandably move on to the next priority. The workload, however, rarely stays still. Traffic patterns evolve, prompts grow longer, serving engines such as vLLM ship new releases, SageMaker inference develops new optimization techniques, and new fine-tuned checkpoints change the resources your model needs. Over time, a well-tuned endpoint quietly drifts. Latency and time to first token edge upward. A configuration that was never quite ideal keeps missing available performance gains. A GPU provisioned for demand that never materialized sits idle week after week. Because nothing has failed, no alarm sounds, and the drift goes unnoticed until users feel it or the bill reflects it. Amazon SageMaker AI now monitors your generative AI inference endpoints and tells you when a change could improve performance or lower cost by using Generative AI optimized inference recommendations feature with Agentic experience in SageMaker JupyterLab. Monitoring is on by default for SageMaker AI inference endpoints using vLLM serving containers and GPU instances, with no setup required, and you can opt out of endpoints. SageMaker AI looks only at operational signals: latency, GPU utilization, and the endpoint’s serving configuration. It does not read your requests or responses. From those signals, it surfaces three kinds of findings: Latency drift: A week-over-week rise in median (p50) end-to-end latency or time to first token. Unused capacity: GPUs you pay for that sit mostly idle. Configuration gaps: A serving container that’s missing newer performance improvements or security patches, or an optimization such as speculative decoding or GPU kernel tuning that your model supports but the endpoint doesn’t use. SageMaker AI sends a finding through AWS Health, with one notification per endpoint that covers that endpoint’s findings. When a notification arrives, you can act on it in one place. It opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in Amazon SageMaker Studio with the endpoint, and its recent traffic already filled in. From there, you run inference recommendations to benchmark your current configuration against alternatives and compare them side by side on response time, throughput, and cost per million tokens. That turns a judgment call into a decision backed by data. Benchmarks run on separate compute, and nothing changes on your endpoint until you choose to apply a result. In this post, we show how SageMaker AI monitors your endpoints and how to read the notifications it sends through AWS Health. We then show how to go from a notification to a benchmarked decision in SageMaker Studio. We walk through three example scenarios, show how to apply or dismiss a recommendation safely, and explain how to opt an endpoint out of monitoring. Solution overview SageMaker AI inference recommendations follow a four-step loop: observe, notify, recommend, and decide. Each step is designed so that you stay in control, and your production endpoint isn’t changed without your explicit action. Observe – Monitoring of latency and capacity usage is on by default for eligible endpoints. It doesn’t read your requests or responses, and it carries no additional GPU cost. Notify – When there is something worth acting on, you receive a plain language notification in AWS Health, plus email, explaining what was observed, why it matters, and a recommended next step. Recommend (opt in) – One selection opens the SageMaker AI agentic experience in SageMaker Studio, prefilled with the endpoint and its observed traffic, so you can benchmark alternatives on separate compute. Decide – Compare response time, throughput, and cost side by side. Production is not changed until you apply a result. The feature produces a few types of findings. The following table summarizes what triggers each one and what gets tested when you choose to benchmark. Finding What triggers it What a benchmark tests Latency drift Response time moves relative to the endpoint’s week-over-week trends Tensor parallelism settings and alternate instance types or sizes Underutilized GPUs GPU utilization stays well below capacity over the window Cheaper instance types and smaller sizes at observed peak traffic Speculative decoding not enabled Model and container support it, but it is off (configuration based) Current configuration compared to speculative decoding enabled Serving container The endpoint’s serving container has a newer version with a performance improvement and security patches for critical and high finding Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). Current compared to updated container Untuned GPU kernels Kernel configuration is not tuned for the model and hardware Default compared to tuned kernels Prerequisites Monitoring itself needs no setup, it is on by default. The following prerequisites apply when you choose to act on a finding by running a benchmark and, optionally, applying a change: Access to AWS Health and the AWS User Notifications console. A SageMaker Studio domain and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to run inference recommendation jobs and update endpoints. Sufficient service quota for the benchmark instances you want to test. Cost note: Monitoring has no GPU cost. Benchmarks use standard SageMaker AI charges, or your machine learning (ML) reservation if you have one. Understand a finding notification You receive notifications in AWS Health on the console and by email and each one follows the same structure, so it’s quick to scan: Endpoint: Which endpoint the finding applies to. What we noticed: The observation, stated plainly, with estimates clearly labeled as estimates. Why it matters: The impact on latency, capacity, or cost. Recommended action: A single selection into the agentic experience in SageMaker Studio to investigate. Notifications report observations and label estimates. No benchmark has run at this point. A representative notification reads as follows: Subject: [Action may be required] SageMaker AI inference improvements for your endpoint SageMaker AI tracks the latency and capacity usage of your inference endpoints by default, and found improvements for one of them. It does not read your requests or responses. What we noticed: Over the past week, time to first token on this endpoint increased compared with the week before. Recommended action: Open SageMaker Studio to benchmark alternatives on separate compute. Your production endpoint is not changed. Cadence: Each endpoint gets one notification that covers the applicable findings. You get at most one notification per endpoint at a time, covering all its findings, and SageMaker AI limits how many an account receives at once. Notifications are AWS Region specific, so you see an endpoint’s findings when you’re signed in to that endpoint’s Region. Walkthrough: From notification to decision In this section, we review a few scenarios of endpoint optimizations that will trigger findings to be reported. Scenario 1: Catch week-over-week latency regression A team runs a chat assistant on a single SageMaker AI endpoint. They add retrieval to improve answer quality, so every request now carries pages of retrieved context and prompts get much longer. Nothing breaks, and no alarm they set trips, but responses start more slowly. SageMaker AI compares the endpoint’s median (p50) time to first token and median end-to-end latency with the previous week. When either one rises enough over the week, it flags the change. Because the comparison is against the endpoint’s own history, the team doesn’t need to set a threshold in advance. Notification: AWS Health reports that time to first token increased relative to the prior week. Studio session: One selection opens the agentic experience, prefilled with the endpoint and its observed traffic. Benchmark: The session tests tensor parallelism settings and other instance types or sizes on separate compute. Decision: The team compares latency, throughput, and cost, then applies the winning configuration to one variant. The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for a latency drift finding. The message reports that median time to first token rose about 200 ms week over week, and the Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations. Figure 1: AWS Health event for a latency drift finding, with a link to run inference recommendations in SageMaker AI Scenario 2: Turn on an optimization your traffic can benefit from A platform team hosts an internal code-completion model on a SageMaker AI endpoint. They deployed it with default serving settings and never revisited them. The model and serving container support speculative decoding, a technique for faster responses, but it isn’t enabled. SageMaker AI flags this as an opportunity. Whether it helps depends on the endpoint’s traffic, such as how many requests run concurrently and how long prompts and responses are. The notification recommends running inference recommendations, which benchmarks speculative decoding against the endpoint’s recent traffic and shows whether it’s worth turning on. Notification: AWS Health reports that a technique designed to make responses faster is supported but not enabled. Studio session: The agentic experience opens with the endpoint configuration loaded. Benchmark: The session compares the current configuration with speculative decoding enabled. Results may differ at peak compared to off-peak traffic. Decision: If the gain holds at the traffic that matters, the team applies it. Otherwise, they keep the current configuration. The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for a speculative decoding finding. The message reports that the model and serving container support speculative decoding, but the endpoint doesn’t use it. The Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations. Figure 2: AWS Health event for a speculative decoding finding, with a link to run inference recommendations in SageMaker AI The notification explains that speculative decoding can make responses faster, and that the benchmark compares response time with and without it on the endpoint’s recent traffic. Scenario 3: Right-size underutilized GPUs A summarization endpoint was sized for a launch that drew a fraction of the planned audience, so its GPUs sit mostly idle for a week. This scenario also shows a case where the right decision may be to make no change at all. Notification: AWS Health reports that the endpoint paid for GPU capacity that largely went unused. Studio session: The agentic experience opens with the endpoint and its observed peak traffic. Benchmark: The session tests cheaper instance types and smaller sizes at observed peak traffic. Decision: The team weighs the monthly savings against the headroom they want for planned growth and may decide to keep the current size. The following screenshot shows an AWS Health event for an unused capacity finding. The message reports that for most of the week, even the endpoint’s busiest GPU used 12 percent or less of its capacity. The Recommended actions pane links to SageMaker AI to run inference recommendations. Figure 3: AWS Health event for an unused capacity finding, with a link to run inference recommendations in SageMaker AI You can choose Open in SageMaker AI from the recommended actions as shown in the screenshot above to apply or dismiss a recommendation. Lets walk through this in next section. Apply or dismiss a recommendation You stay in control throughout, and nothing deploys automatically. When you choose Open in SageMaker AI from a notification’s recommended actions, Amazon SageMaker Studio opens a JupyterLab space and shows the prompt that will run in the agentic chat. The following screenshot shows the prompt for a latency drift finding on an endpoint that also runs an older vLLM serving container: When you choose Run, the agentic experience opens in a chat panel in JupyterLab space in SageMaker Studio. It summarizes the finding in plain language, restates what you asked it to do, and checks with you before it takes any action. The following screenshot shows the agent summarizing the findings and asking to continue: After you confirm, the agent generates a notebook that creates an inference recommendation job for the endpoint. The notebook uses the SageMaker Python SDK, takes the model from the endpoint and the traffic profile from its metrics, and tags the job with the AWS Health event so you can trace the results back to the finding. Each step is a separate notebook cell, so you can review or edit it before you run it. The following screenshot shows the notebook cells that record the job details and start a recommendation job across three candidate instance types. When the job completes, you can compare your current configuration with the alternatives on response time, throughput, and cost. When you are ready to act on a benchmarked result, we recommend a safe rollout pattern: Review the proposed change before applying it, including the configuration difference and the benchmarked latency, throughput, and cost. Apply to one production variant first and keep the current configuration available for rollback. Holding or dismissing a finding is a normal outcome. The notification stays in your AWS Health event history. Manage monitoring and notifications You can manage monitoring and how you are notified: Manage how you receive notifications in the AWS User Notifications console. Optionally, schedule recurring recommendations, for example monthly. What is and is not collected: Monitoring reads aggregated latency and capacity telemetry at the endpoint level. It doesn’t read your request or response content, and it carries no GPU cost. Opting out of monitoring: If you don’t want SageMaker AI to monitor an endpoint, set the OPT_OUT_TRACKING environment variable, with a value of your choice, on the model’s container. You set it in the Environment map when you call CreateModel, either on PrimaryContainer or on another container in the model. If a container on the endpoint carries this variable, SageMaker AI collects no monitoring telemetry for that endpoint, including engine metrics, GPU metrics, and startup configuration details. As a result, it sends no notifications for that endpoint. Clean up To avoid ongoing charges, clean up the resources you created while following this post: Delete any test endpoints or resources you created for the walkthrough. Remove benchmark artifacts in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), if applicable. Revert any test configuration changes you applied. Conclusion With SageMaker AI inference recommendations now monitoring your endpoints automatically, optimization moves from a point-in-time snapshot to an ongoing signal. Your endpoints keep telling you when they have drifted, when they are missing an improvement, or when they are paying for idle capacity. A single selection takes you to a benchmarked, side-by-side decision that you control. For more information on how to get started, visit Amazon SageMaker AI and see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation. About the authors Hazim Qudah Hazim is a Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS based in Dallas, TX. He enjoys helping customers build and adopt AI/ML solutions using AWS technologies and best practices. Prior to his role at AWS, he spent many years in technology consulting with customers across many industries and geographies. In his free time, he enjoys cooking, staying active, and playing with his dog Nala. Mona Mona Mona is a Worldwide Specialist Solutions Architect for AI/ML at AWS, based in the Washington, D.C. area. She works with customers to design and deploy generative AI inference on Amazon SageMaker AI, focusing on model optimization, cost efficiency, and production best practices. She is a frequent speaker and author on applied machine learning and co-leads the Women in AI/ML community. Vineet Sharma Vineet is a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Tech at AWS, focused on Amazon SageMaker AI. He specializes in go-to-market strategy, product launches, and translating complex AI and ML services into compelling customer value. He is passionate about creating great customer experiences through clear, impactful messaging. Li Zhang Li is a Senior Machine Learning Engineer at AWS, working on Amazon SageMaker AI inference. Li leads and builds the system that monitors customers generative AI inference endpoints and recommends changes that improve their performance and cost. Over 11 years at Amazon, Li has built large-scale distributed systems and machine learning services.

items.title: Enable AI agents to pay for AWS Marketplace x402 products with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments
items.summary: When Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments became generally available in August 2026, agents could autonomously pay for paid APIs, MCP servers, and web content over open protocols like x402 and MPP with payment limits and full observability. Today we extend that autonomy to AWS Marketplace, so agents can discover and buy x402-enabled software, APIs, data, and content, and pay in USD on the agent developer’s AWS bill, removing the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys. Figure 1: Overview of AgentCore payments showing the new AWS Billing integration for purchasing on AWS Marketplace Developers can also configure and automate discovery through the AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. Existing guardrails carry over, developers can set spending limits and approved sellers using AgentCore policy, and the payment session cap is enforced by AgentCore payments, so an agent is unable to overspend. Transactions are auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. Because agent purchases run through AWS accounts on both sides, agentic purchasing meets the security and auditability enterprises expect. The x402 catalog on AWS Marketplace is expanding with a growing roster of trusted, verified sellers. Tavily, a live search provider for agentic commerce, is one of them: Agentic commerce isn’t just about giving agents the ability to pay. It’s about giving enterprises the confidence to let them. That conviction is driving Tavily’s collaboration with the AWS team on the design of Agentic Commerce. By bringing secure, x402 powered transactions to AWS Marketplace and connecting agents with trusted, KYC verified providers, AWS is laying the foundation for autonomous commerce at production scale. This is what enterprise ready agentic commerce looks like. — Rotem Weiss, Founder & CEO, Tavily What’s launching today Today’s launch adds AWS Billing as a payment option in AgentCore payments. An agent can now pay x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers per request, in USD, settling on their AWS bill. When an AWS Marketplace seller responds with 402 Payment Required, its response includes a signed quote for the purchase. With AWS Billing, the agent can forward the seller’s x402 response to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks session budgets, then returns a payment token. The agent retries the request to the seller with the payment token included and receives a successful response. AWS bills the charge to the AWS account where Payment Manager is set up, and the charge appears on that account’s AWS bill. To set up AWS Marketplace purchasing, the developer creates a Payment Manager with an AWS Billing connector. The connector only requires you to set up a service-linked role to access AWS Marketplace. Then, for each task, developers can create a payment session with a spending limit and give the agent the session ID. An agent’s first purchase from a seller creates an agreement for the AWS account with that seller, and AWS Marketplace automatically tracks later purchases against it. Each product will then show up as an AWS Marketplace line item. If your organization uses Private Marketplace, agents can only buy the products it allows. In addition, to discover new sellers, we are launching a new AWS Marketplace connector in AgentCore Gateway. This optional integration helps agents find products and their endpoints. At launch, AWS Billing supports the x402 exact scheme, where the seller quotes a fixed price for each request. In this post, we walk through a research agent that discovers a tool, pays for a single request through AWS Billing, and answers with sources, with nothing set up in advance. We also provide an accompanying GitHub sample that you can use to evaluate the setup in your own AWS account. Sample walkthrough Suppose a financial analyst asks the agent what was announced about agentic payments this week. The model wasn’t trained on this week’s news, so the agent looks for a search tool. Through AgentCore Gateway, it searches AWS Marketplace, reads the listing from Tavily, an AWS Marketplace seller, and requests the listing’s x402 endpoints. The agent calls the endpoint and receives an x402 payload with price details. The agent then forwards the x402 payload to AgentCore payments. AgentCore payments checks it against the remaining session budget and returns a payment token. Once these checks are passed, the agent sends the request again with the token attached, and gets the search results. Its answer includes sources and states what it bought and what it cost. In this workflow, agents can apply their reasoning to decide which AWS Marketplace tool to use. How it works Figure 2: End-to-end flow of the sample solution using a Strands agent 1. Discover. The agent calls three read-only gateway tools in order: search listings, get a listing, and list its fulfillment options. Search listings tool only returns endpoints that accept x402. The last call returns the seller’s endpoint URL and the payment protocols it accepts. 2. Get a quote. The agent calls the endpoint with no payment attached. The seller answers with HTTP 402 and puts a signed quote in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header. AWS Marketplace checks the signature against the seller’s registered key, which means a quote with an altered price gets rejected. 3. Pay. The agent passes the quote to the ProcessPayment API with the payment type AWS_BILLING_X402. If budget remains in the session, AgentCore payments issues a payment token. If not, the call fails and the developer is not charged. 4. Redeem. The agent sends the request again, this time with the token in the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header, and the seller returns the content. Payment tokens are valid for about five minutes, so the agent completes steps 2 through 4 in a single pass. 5. Settle. On the developer’s first purchase from a seller, AWS Marketplace creates the agreement with that seller. After that it meters each charge to their AWS bill. Settlement runs asynchronously and shows up in their AWS bill monthly. Prerequisites To create an AWS Billing connector, developers’ AWS accounts must have the AWS Marketplace service-linked role AWSServiceRoleForMarketplaceAgenticCommerce. AWS Marketplace uses this role to bill AWS Marketplace purchases that their agents make to their AWS account. Refer to the documentation for more details. Hands-on The open-source GitHub sample in the agentcore-samples repository runs through a demo of the new functionality. It can help you configure AgentCore payments for AWS Marketplace, connect Tavily, run the agent, and inspect the transaction. You can refer to the documentation for more details. Step 1: Configure AgentCore payments setup_aws_billing.py creates a payment manager with an AWS Billing connector, plus the AWS Marketplace service-linked role and three separate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. The session role can set budgets but can’t pay. Meanwhile the agent role can pay but can’t create sessions, so the agent has no way to raise its own budget. python setup_aws_billing.py --region us-east-1 Step 2: Connect Tavily setup_gateway.py creates an AgentCore Gateway with the AWS Marketplace connector and gives the agent role the appropriate permissions to use it. The gateway’s role is limited to three read-only AWS Marketplace actions. If you choose to skip this step, you can instead set SELLER_URL in the environment variables to the seller’s endpoint, and the agent will pay that URL only rather than using AgentCore Gateway discovery. python setup_gateway.py --region us-east-1 Step 3: Run the agent The script creates a payment session as the session role and then runs the agent as the agent role. By default the session budget is $0.05 and the per-request cap is $0.02. python strands_marketplace_agent.py "What was announced about agentic payments this week? Cite sources." The agent searches, looks at listings, gets an endpoint, and pays once. In this test run against a $0.01 seller, it compared two listings before buying: Tool calls: search_marketplace -> get_remaining_budget -> search_marketplace -> search_marketplace -> get_listing -> get_listing -> get_seller_endpoints -> get_seller_endpoints -> fetch_paid_api -> get_remaining_budget Payments this run: 1, total $0.01 Step 4: Inspect the transaction When the run finishes, the sample will print the payment with its amount, AWS Marketplace product ID, and processPaymentId. The AWS Marketplace meters charges asynchronously, so the Tavily line item takes a moment to appear on your bill. Agent purchases will also show up in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. Step 5: Clean up Run cleanup.py to delete resources. Make sure to validate deletion to avoid incurring additional resource charges. Conclusion AgentCore payments and AWS Marketplace provide the infrastructure for agents that can transact. The research agent in this post goes from “I need live web search” to sourcing an answer on its own, discovering premium paid content through tools, and paying for requests that settle on the developer’s AWS bill. With AgentCore payments, developers can build with open protocols like x402, which opens them to a growing catalog of trusted, verified AWS Marketplace sellers. This gives agents more autonomy and developers more control. Governance is built in, with per-session spending caps and an approved seller list using AgentCore policy, and IAM identities that make it auditable in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer. The agent chooses the right tool for the task, and developers can keep the same billing, budgets, and controls they already trust. Resources AgentCore payments documentation. GitHub sample. AWS Marketplace seller documentation. x402-enabled products in AWS Marketplace. AWS Marketplace launch blog post. About the authors Madhu Samhitha Vangara Madhu is a Worldwide generative AI Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS, focusing on Agentic AI technical GTM for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and Strands Agents. She brings deep enterprise experience translating emerging AI capabilities into measurable customer outcomes. Madhu is a speaker at AI conferences and specializes in production-grade Agentic AI. Khusbu Mishra Khusbu is a Senior Software Development Engineer at AWS, based in Seattle, WA. She is a core member of the engineering team that built and launched Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments, which enables AI agents to make secure payments. With over 8 years of experience building fintech solutions, Khusbu has worked on greenfield projects including building payment gateway, integrating with payment providers, and building a real-time solution that detects and mitigates payment partner availability issues. She is passionate about emerging agentic commerce and how AI agents will shape the future of the digital economy – how AI agents can discover, pay for, and transact with services on their own, safely and at scale. Joshua Smith Joshua is a Principal Solutions Architect at AWS who works with fintech customers. He helps them build secure, reliable, cost-effective, AI-enabled solutions, such as agentic commerce integrations. Chidambaram Muthappan Chidambaram is a Senior Specialist Solutions Architect on the AWS Marketplace team. He helps partners bring their products to customers in AWS Marketplace. Anil Nadiminti Anil is the North America Geo Leader for Agentic AI in the AI/ML Technical Field Community at AWS and a Senior Solutions Architect focused on FinTech within Financial Services. He designs scalable, interoperable multi-agent systems and partners with global financial institutions and blockchain-native companies to build and scale solutions across Web3, digital assets, and decentralized finance. He is a frequent speaker on agentic AI and agentic commerce at industry events and contributes to open-source projects and blogs.
