items.title: From learning to leaderboard: How Cisco upskilled 1,200 engineers in agentic AI with AWS AI League
items.summary: Cisco, like many large engineering organizations, is adopting generative and agentic AI to change how its engineers build software. The hard part is no longer access to the technology. It’s helping thousands of engineers move from watching a demo to confidently building with it. Recorded sessions and slide decks rarely close that gap. Engineers learn fastest when they build something real, see it fail, fix it, and try again. AWS designed AWS AI League for exactly that. It turns hands-on AI learning into a gamified competition, where participants customize models and build agents on AWS, get instant feedback on a live leaderboard, and compete in a game-show-style finale. Cisco is one of the clearest examples of what this looks like at scale. In 2025, Hemanth V, a Cisco software engineer, went from an internal Cisco event to being crowned the first AWS AI League Champion at AWS re:Invent 2025. In 2026, 1,200 Cisco engineers competed in an AWS AI League tournament at Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0. The winner, Nishanth Aluhonnu, earned a full event pass to AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas. In this post, we share how Cisco and AWS used Cisco Transformation Fest and AWS AI League to build a lasting culture of learning by doing. We previously covered this program in From theory to delivery: How Atos upskilled 400 engineers in agentic AI, and here we look at Cisco’s experience. We walk through Cisco’s journey, share technical lessons from the 2026 winning agent, and explain how your organization can host its own AWS AI League. What is AWS AI League? AWS AI League helps organizations build advanced AI skills through competition. Each league follows three steps: Learn – A hands-on, 2-hour workshop led by AWS experts introduces the tools and the challenge. Build – Participants experiment at their own pace and submit to a live leaderboard, with an automated evaluator giving real-time feedback after each submission. Compete – Top finalists take the stage in a live, game-show-style grand finale. Although AWS AI League offers multiple use cases, at Cisco it offered the following two challenges: Agentic AI challenge – Participants build agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. The agents move through a maze-like grid, solving challenges on the way to a treasure chest. The challenges map to real-world tasks such as handling inappropriate content, running code, retrieving information from the web, and extracting structured data. Builders can choose models for supervisor and sub-agents and add tools such as AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and AWS Lambda Event Functions. Builders use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply safety controls to their agents. Model customization challenge – Participants fine-tune models in Amazon SageMaker Studio using the latest training recipes. The challenge awards points when an automated evaluator rates a participant’s customized model as more accurate and comprehensive than a reference model on the specific tasks in the competition. Finalists are scored on time efficiency, accuracy, agent planning, and token consumption efficiency. Figure 1: AWS AI League champion at AWS re:Invent 2025 Figure 2: 2026 AWS AI League winner at Cisco campus The Cisco and AWS partnership The AWS AI League story at Cisco grows out of a deep engineering partnership. Cisco and AWS bring together networking, cloud, security, and observability for shared customers including: Cisco SD-WAN, whose controller architecture runs on AWS and serves customers globally as a software as a service (SaaS) application. Cisco Meraki, Cisco Spaces, and Cisco’s IoT and smart buildings group. Cisco Cloud Control, a cloud-native, AI-powered application integrated with AWS services that brings together security, networking, observability, and collaboration. Cisco AI Defense, where Cisco’s security team uses Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI to embed AI governance and guardrails across the Cisco portfolio. The two companies have also published joint deployment guides and Cisco Validated Designs across networking and AWS. A recent example of co-innovation is SD-WAN fabric on demand across the AWS backbone, built to deliver the resilience and uptime customers expect. “When you see that many business units independently choosing to build their next-generation platforms natively on AWS, that’s not a vendor relationship anymore. It’s a true engineering partnership.” — Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco Cisco’s VP of Engineering Kumaril Kapoor and AWS Industries India leader Chandra Balani sit down to discuss the AWS and Cisco partnership story, from co-innovation across networking, cloud, and AI to enabling thousands of engineers through the annual Cisco AWS Transformation Fest. Cisco Transformation Fest: Enablement at scale As the partnership grew, it extended beyond technology to people. Working closely with Cisco teams in India, AWS saw a strong appetite for learning and experimenting among Cisco engineers across many business units. The question was how to scale that impact beyond the day-to-day touchpoints of the partnership. The answer was Cisco Transformation Fest, first held in 2022. The program is built on five tenets the team summarized as SCALE: Tenet What it means for Cisco engineers Share Share what you know with peers across teams. Connect Connect with engineers across business units. Adopt Adopt new skills and AWS services. Learn Learn by building, not by watching. Experiment / Engage Experiment hands-on and stay engaged with the technology and each other. Figure 3: 2026 Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 4.0 AWS AI League finalists Transformation Fest brings together several formats: AWS GameDays, AWS AI League, sessions where Cisco leaders share best practices and success stories with peers, and sessions on Amazon and AWS culture. What began as a single event is now an annual, three-day program that has completed its fourth edition and reached around 2,000 engineers. AWS continues to engage Cisco teams with hands-on workshops and experience-based accelerations. “It has been genuinely valuable for us, and it’s really a journey, but I appreciate most is the intent behind it. It’s built around our people. It gives our engineers the time, the space, and the hands-on support to grow real skills on AWS. For us, it has turned into a lasting culture of learning by doing. It’s not a one-off event.” — Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco Where enablement becomes execution: AWS AI League at Cisco Of all the Transformation Fest formats, AWS AI League has had the most visible impact. Its gamified, hands-on structure puts engineers to work with Amazon SageMaker on fine-tuning, model customization and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for agent building, against a clock and in front of their peers. Participants leave with practical experience and genuine confidence in their AI skills. “This is where enablement actually turns into real execution.” — Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco 2025: From the Cisco campus to global champion Hemanth V, a software engineer in Cisco’s switching core platform team, had an inspiring journey that set the benchmark for Cisco. His journey had two stages: AWS AI League at Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 3.0. He competed against more than 600 participants from Cisco in a model customization challenge, fine-tuning a small model in Amazon SageMaker, and won the title. Global grand finale at AWS re:Invent 2025. In Las Vegas he faced a completely different challenge: the agentic AI track, where he built an agent to navigate a dynamic, game-style maze. He took first place and was recognized during the re:Invent keynote. Hemanth finished ahead of Ross Williams from Aqfer (second place) and Deepesh Khanna from Capital One (third place). “You don’t need to know everything beforehand. You will learn a lot of things on the way. The only thing that matters is your curiosity and willingness to learn.” — Hemanth V, Software Engineer, Cisco, and 2025 AWS AI League Champion 2026: 1,200 engineers, one champion In 2026, Cisco Transformation Fest 4.0 hosted a full AWS AI League agentic AI tournament. The AWS account team ran pre-event training so that engineers with no prior agentic AI experience could compete from day one. The format was designed to narrow a large field down to a single winner: Stage Format Winning result Qualifier 1,200 participants across four cohorts. Top 5 per cohort advance to semifinal 1st in cohort 3 with 15,906 points (98 submissions) Semifinal 20 participants compete for 3 finalist spots 1st with 16,321 points Finale 3 live rounds on stage in front of Cisco and AWS leadership 1st with 27,008 cumulative points Nishanth Aluhonnu, a software engineer at Cisco, finished first at every stage and earned a full conference pass to AWS re:Invent 2026. The finale itself showed why the format works. Participants could not change code, tools, or prompts during the finale, only a short steering instruction before each round. Success depended on how well each agent made decisions on maps it had never seen before. Nishanth lost the first round, then won the second by a wide margin by ignoring a board full of low-value coins in favor of a single high-value challenge. Figure 4: Cisco AWS Transformation Fest 4.0 AWS AI League finalists on stage Examining what it takes to win an agentic AI challenge The 2026 winning agent offers lessons that go well beyond the game. Each design choice maps to a decision teams face when they run agents in production. Output tokens are the real cost The agentic AI challenge scores agents on challenge points, a treasure bonus, remaining lives, and a token bonus, computed as tokenBonus = 1000 - (totalOutputTokens / challengesVisited). In the qualifier, the top four agents all solved the map. The first-place agent emitted 1,220 output tokens and the second-place agent emitted 1,430, and the final margin was only 16 points out of nearly 16,000. After every agent can solve the problem, efficiency decides the winner. To understand which tokens mattered, Nishanth built nine variants of the same agent, changing one thing at a time. The result was clear: tool results and the system prompt didn’t count against the score, but everything the agent wrote, including tool call arguments, did. Each tool call carried roughly 52 tokens of fixed overhead on top of its arguments. This mirrors real-world cost. Generating output is sequential and is typically priced several times higher than input, and in an agent loop that cost compounds across every step. A long, well-structured system prompt (which you can also cache) is cheap. A chatty agent isn’t. One agent, not five A common architecture for this challenge is a supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that delegates to specialist sub-agents for navigation, computation, and web retrieval. It’s a sound pattern for many production systems. The winning design used a single agent with no sub-agents. Instead, the prompt began with a short dispatch table that matched each challenge type to the right approach in a single turn. The reasoning was simple: every handoff between agents is a message the model has to write, and in this challenge every written token is scored. The lesson isn’t that sub-agents are bad. It’s to choose your architecture based on what coordination costs you. When coordination is expensive, a flatter design can win. The following diagram shows the AWS reference architecture for the agentic AI challenge: a supervisor agent with specialist sub-agents. The winning design deliberately didn’t use this multi-agent pattern. Figure 5: AWS AI League reference architecture In this reference architecture, a supervisor agent runs in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and coordinates three sub-agents, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and AgentCore memory connected to the runtime. The supervisor and sub-agents route through the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to four tools: a navigation tool, browser tool, code execution tool, and custom tools using AWS Lambda functions. Put deterministic logic in tools Route planning was not left to the model. It ran in an AWS Lambda function that treated the board as an optimization problem. Each tile carried an expected value: the points it paid, minus the lives it could cost, minus the tokens the agent would spend to solve it. The planner respected constraints, such as collecting a key before its door, and refined the route within a time budget. This is a useful pattern for most agents: let the model handle language and judgment, and move search, math, and rules into tools where they are faster, cheaper, and repeatable. Make decisions on value, not habit The second finale round was designed as a trap. A seven-by-seven board was almost entirely covered in coins worth 25 points each, while a single scheduling challenge tile was worth 1,500 points. Habit said to collect the coins. The planner’s value table said the coins were noise. The agent went for the high-value challenge and scored 7,537 points in that round, compared with 5,953 for the next finalist. That round built the lead that carried the agent to the overall win. Impact for Cisco Across two years of AWS AI League at Cisco, the impact shows up in skills, culture, and recognition: Hands-on AI skills at scale. 1,200 engineers took part in the 2026 tournament, building agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, many of them with no prior agentic AI experience. Connections across business units. Engineers who would otherwise never have met competed in the same tournament, shared approaches, and learned from each other. A lasting culture of learning. Now in its fourth year, Transformation Fest has become an annual commitment rather than a one-off hackathon. Recognition, two years in a row. A Cisco engineer won the 2025 AWS AI League global title, and the 2026 Cisco champion will attend AWS re:Invent 2026. Leadership visibility. The 2026 finale took place in front of Cisco and AWS senior leadership, giving engineers a real stage for their work. For Hemanth, the biggest takeaway was confidence. You do not need to master everything before you start. You learn by getting hands-on. “Technology alone isn’t enough. You need people who are empowered to experiment with it. Transformation Fest created that enablement environment, and AWS AI League created the opportunity for execution.” — Kumaril Kapoor, VP of Engineering, Cisco Conclusion In this post, we showed how Cisco and AWS turned enablement into execution. Cisco Transformation Fest created a space for engineers to learn by doing, and AWS AI League gave them a real challenge, a scoreboard, and a stage. The result is a culture of hands-on AI building that reaches thousands of engineers. To get started: Learn how to host a tournament in your organization on the AWS AI League page. Build your agentic AI and model customization skills with the AWS AI training catalog on AWS Skill Builder. Follow the AWS AI League 2026 global finale at AWS re:Invent 2026 in Las Vegas. We look forward to seeing what your teams build. About the authors Rakesh Vangari Rakesh is a Principal Account Executive at Amazon Web Services (AWS), based in Hyderabad, India. He has more than 20 years of experience across sales, strategy and technology. At AWS, he leads strategic global technology partnerships and works with executives to connect business outcomes to cloud and generative AI decisions. He helps customers take AI from pilot to production and build various mechanisms that help engineering teams to build and deploy on AWS for their customers. His approach: solve first, earn trust and deliver results. Biswanath Mukherjee Biswanath is a Senior Solutions Architect at Amazon Web Services. He works with large strategic customers of AWS by providing them technical guidance to migrate-modernize their applications and build agentic AI solutions on AWS Cloud. With his extensive cross industry experience in cloud architecture, he partners with customers to develop innovative solutions that follows the scalability, reliability, and agility of AWS best practices to meet their business needs. Madhukiran J Madhukiran is a Sr. Technical Account Manager at AWS Enterprise Support. He supports enterprise customers leveraging AWS services like Amazon Bedrock, AgentCore, and SageMaker to build innovative solutions. His expertise spans Machine Learning, GenAI, and Containers. He has supported multiple customer organizations through AWS AI League Agentic challenges with contribution spanning across APJ events. Ruchi Bhatia Ruchi is a Technical Product Marketing Manager at Amazon Web Services, where she drives product marketing for model training and customization on Amazon SageMaker AI and leads marketing for the AWS AI League. She holds a master’s degree in Information Systems Management from Carnegie Mellon University and is the youngest triple Kaggle Grandmaster across the Notebooks, Datasets, and Discussion categories. Her expertise has led to speaking invitations at Google Cloud Next, NVIDIA GTC, and the University of Oxford, and she is passionate about mentoring early-career professionals breaking into the tech industry. Rajesh Babu Nuvvula Rajesh is a Senior Solutions Architect on the Worldwide Public Sector team at Amazon Web Services (AWS), collaborating with public sector partners and customers to design and scale well-architected solutions for cloud migration and application modernization. His areas of expertise include distributed enterprise applications, data and analytics, AI/ML, and databases. Outside of work, Rajesh enjoys exploring emerging technologies and long walks. Hemanth V Hemanth is a Software Engineer at Cisco, working on the core switching platform team, contributing to IOS XE software development for Cisco Catalyst 9500 and 9600 Series switches. He also develops internal tools to streamline workflows and improve engineering productivity. Outside work, he enjoys tinkering with technology and electronics, building things for fun, and watching movies. Nishanth D Aluhonnu Nishanth is a Software Engineer specializing in DevOps, cloud infrastructure, observability, automation, and large-scale distributed systems. He is passionate about automation and emerging technologies including agentic AI and intelligent systems to simplify infrastructure operations, enhance monitoring, and enable automated root cause analysis. He enjoys strategy games like Dota, solving Capture the Flag (CTF) challenges, and exploring cybersecurity.

items.title: GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra review: should you switch?
items.summary: It’s felt like a while since we had a new Astra to test. Our last GPT-6 Astra evaluation was a little over two months ago. OpenAI has kept shipping, including GPT-6 Cyber, while the improvements in Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 made returning to Claude feel like a good decision. We’re asking agents to handle larger projects and work for hours at a time. Always-on agents such as Dots and Grok Bot can start delegated work from an event, then notify us when results are ready or our input is needed. As that work grows, token usage and the cost of finishing a task become harder to ignore. OpenAI says its new GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra can handle demanding tasks with fewer output tokens. Much of the release conversation focused on image and video generation, so we wanted to see what that meant for software development. We evaluated two uses separately: Code generation, where the models built and changed software. Code review, where they inspected existing pull requests inside CodeRabbit’s pipeline. Could either become our daily coding model or earn a place in our review harness? Selected coding-related releases, September to November 2026. Summaries describe OpenAI’s announced focus, not comparable benchmark scores. Spacing does not represent elapsed time. OpenAI announcements and API changelog Code review: benchmark results We evaluated the final comments produced by CodeRabbit’s review pipeline, after verification and filtering. As we explained in how we bring a model online at CodeRabbit, finding a possible issue and deciding to publish it are separate jobs. A known issue counts as caught when at least one regular actionable comment matches it. Nitpicks and outside-diff comments don’t qualify. Benchmark precision is the share of regular actionable comments that match known issues. Unmatched comments still need to be read to judge their accuracy. Sol 6.2 versus Sol 6.1 We tested Sol on 81 known issues across 42 pull requests. The table brings together coverage, comment volume, recorded cost, and review time. The Sol 6.1 baseline also uses other models in the pipeline. The low- and high-reasoning runs replaced different models in different parts of that pipeline, so they don’t isolate the effect of reasoning level. MeasureSol 6.1, high reasoningSol 6.2, low reasoningSol 6.2, high reasoning Known issues caught, full 81-issue set58 of 81 (71.6%)59 of 81 (72.8%)60 of 81 (74.1%) Regular actionable comments187202290 Total nitpicks111133 Benchmark precision35.3%32.7%25.9% Mean recorded cost per review$0.772$0.830$1.146 Median full-review time7m 49s7m 44s7m 53s Sol 6.2 at high reasoning caught two more known issues across the full set. Each configuration ran once, and the gain includes changes outside the part where we replaced Sol, so it does not establish a reliable model-only improvement. Sol 6.2’s high-reasoning run had a recorded cost about 48% higher than the baseline, while median review time changed by four seconds. Frozen upstream calls used recorded responses at zero provider cost, and the remaining calls ran live. These figures describe replay-run costs and full-pipeline timings. They do not establish production review costs or the latency of code generation tasks. Astra 6.2 versus Astra 6 MeasureGPT-6 AstraGPT-6.2 Astra Known issues caught51 of 83 (61.5%)58 of 83 (69.9%) Reported comments331847 Actionable-comment benchmark precision21.74%12.22% Nitpick/assertive comments5215 Standard API input price, per million tokens$10$8 Cached API input price, per million tokens$1$0.40 Standard API output price, per million tokens$50$40 GPT-6.2 Astra’s 847 reported comments include 589 regular actionable comments and 258 findings in summary sections. GPT-6 Astra’s comment total has not been reconciled to those categories. Nitpick/assertive comments are separate. These results do not establish a model-only improvement between the Astra versions. In the 83-issue benchmark, the baseline configuration used Sol 6.1 for most scored issues, alongside other models. It caught 54 of 83 known issues, compared with the Astra integration’s 58. Astra picked up 11 known issues the baseline missed and missed seven that the baseline caught, leaving a net gain of four. GPT-6.2 Astra configuration’s median review time was 25 seconds longer than its baseline’s 5m 37s, about 7.4%. That measures the full pipeline, including verification, and cannot establish that Astra itself is slower. Only nine of 83 cases had all costs recorded, compared with 58 in that baseline, so the run cannot establish a reliable cost per completed review. According to OpenAI’s pricing announcement, standard input and output API rates fell by 20%, and cached input by 60%. These rates exclude long-context premiums and service-tier adjustments. Lower token prices alone do not establish lower review costs, which also depend on delegated calls and retries. More comments need to earn their place With GPT-6.2 Astra, regular actionable comments increased from the baseline’s 253 to 589. Of those 589 comments, 72 matched known issues. Multiple comments can match the same issue, which is why that count differs from the 58 distinct issues caught. The remaining 517 comments may include useful problems outside the benchmark’s labels. Understanding their value requires reading them. Sol 6.2’s high-reasoning configuration raises the same question. Comments increased from 187 to 290, about 55%, while the full pipeline caught two more known issues overall. We’d inspect the additional comments before treating the higher volume as a benefit. Every additional comment asks someone to separate a useful finding from noise. A PR filled with low-value feedback makes that harder. Authors may eventually stop reading or addressing the comments, leaving useful findings ignored too. Our next experiment would require the reviewer to explain what triggers a problem and what the author would observe before posting an inline comment. We’d then sample both the comments kept and those removed to check whether the filter discards useful findings. As our framework for evaluating AI code review tools explains, the goal is feedback that leads to a meaningful code change. Code generation: our hands-on experience We used both models to build interfaces and work on projects. These are observations from our coding sessions. We didn’t run a matched code-generation benchmark. Astra often produced a useful first interface from a short prompt. It chose layouts without waiting for clarification. Prompt quality was still key when working within an existing design. On longer tasks, Astra returned to the original goal after detours and brought delegated investigations back into the work without us having to restate the brief. Sol 6.2 needed more direction. Its initial UI designs weren’t an improvement over 6.1 in our sessions, and parts of the implementation remained rough even with a reference. Small changes sometimes prompted long pauses before implementation. It also repeatedly gave us incorrect configurations when setting up projects from scratch, so we had to verify that they actually started. Recall and precision across our reviews The chart below shows recall and precision results from this review and our Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 evaluations, ordered from highest to lowest reported recall. The benchmark sets and scoring definitions differ across reviews, so this is not a head-to-head comparison. Model configurationRecallPrecision GPT-6.2 Sol, high reasoning74.1%25.9% GPT-6.2 Sol, low reasoning72.8%32.7% GPT-6.1 Sol, high reasoning71.6%35.3% GPT-6.2 Astra69.9%12.22% Claude Opus 5.5 Standard63.8%38.6% Claude Opus 5.5 Max62.5%35.7% Claude Fable 5.1, low reasoning61.0%37.3% Claude Fable 5.1, high reasoning57.1%36.4% Should you switch for code review? We’d keep the current review defaults while testing both models further. Astra’s additional catches came with a large increase in comments, and the integration needs a comparison with fixed routing. Sol’s small measured gain came with more comments and a higher recorded cost. Before switching, read the additional findings and retest the issues each configuration stopped catching. We’re also working on our Fable 5.2 review.

items.title: How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers
items.summary: When hundreds of agents serve thousands of developers, enterprise governance can’t be an afterthought. At the BMW Group’s R&D, more than 12,500 developers work on approximately 500 million lines of vehicle software code. This software is augmented by the BMW Connected Vehicle backend, a cloud-based system of more than 1,300 microservices providing digital services for 24 million vehicles in the field. In regulated industry, the bar for (software) quality, stability, and governance compliance is exceptionally high. While research, frameworks, and guidelines now facilitate building agents, industrializing and operating high-quality agents in an efficient, scalable manner remains a significant challenge. Scaling agentic AI across a large organization cannot be achieved by isolated teams. It requires collective effort, locally driven experimentation, and active knowledge sharing across the enterprise. This creates a fundamental governance dichotomy: Development teams need the freedom to innovate rapidly, while the enterprise must enforce standards for safety, security, composability, and cost-efficiency. Without that balance, organizations risk a fragmented landscape of AI islands and costly duplicate work. This presents a real challenge given hundreds of globally distributed teams building agents across the BMW Group. In this post, we detail the practices and patterns that support BMW’s R&D teams in building, governing and operating agents at scale without sacrificing speed, quality or compliance. Solution Our premise is straightforward: build agents that can cooperate from the start. This requires an architecture that makes diversity composable, governable, and automatable, without requiring a single framework or toolchain. Central to this architecture is the agent harness, a runtime layer wrapped around a large language model (LLM). It provides the execution loop, tool dispatch, memory management, and observability hooks for autonomous operation. Just as the AWS Well-Architected Framework standardized cloud infrastructure design, agentic systems need equivalent patterns, reusable blueprints encoding governance, composability, and operational best practices from the start. We organize our solution around five interlocking practices, drawn from hands-on experience building and operating agentic systems at enterprise scale since 2023. Each practice is codified as infrastructure as code (IaC), making adoption repeatable, auditable, and enforceable across teams without blocking DevOps velocity. Govern proactively, not retroactively Governance must be structural from the start and maintained across the full lifecycle. We advocate for three properties of effective agentic governance: Framework-agnostic and externalized: Governance rules such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting and content filtering are enforced at the integration layer. This includes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, a central agent registry and orchestration boundary, rather than within individual agent codebases. This means governance survives framework migrations, model swaps, and team reorganizations. Domain-sensitive and graduated: Not every agent action carries the same risk: drafting documentation, updating customer records, and production database writes demand very different levels of oversight. We implement graduated trust through per-step autonomy levels: Level 0 (Human-in-the-loop): Every action requires explicit human approval. This is the starting point for new agents and high-risk operations. Level 1 (Human-on-the-loop): The agent executes autonomously but surfaces decisions for asynchronous human review. Suitable for medium-risk tasks with defined inputs, outputs, and rollback options. Level 2 (Autonomous within guardrails): The agent operates independently within strictly defined policy boundaries, enforced deterministically rather than through prompt instructions (see below). Reserved for low-risk, well-understood operations with verified track records. Assign trust levels per step, not per agent. A single workflow can include steps at all three levels, so teams can start conservatively and incrementally increase autonomy as confidence builds, grounded in measurable evaluation data, not assumptions. Deterministically enforced: Governance runs as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop. In practice, this happens mainly in the CI/CD pipeline. Permission checks, policy-as-code rules, and compliance validations gate every deployment there, before an agent reaches production. Because these checks run separately from the agent, neither the agent nor its prompts are in a position to override them. Egress controls (recipient allowlisting, outbound secret scanning) help prevent an agent holding confidential data from disclosing it through an otherwise legitimate call. Instrument, verify, and evaluate continuously Observability in agentic systems goes beyond traditional application monitoring. The real question is no longer whether a service returned an HTTP 200 status, but whether an agent produced a faithful, policy-compliant output, and how this can be demonstrated through observable execution traces. Answering that requires a ground-truth dataset covering common queries and edge cases. This dataset is used for evaluation from day one, so quality is measured against representative and appropriately governed evaluation datasets for evaluation, not synthetic prompts. This infrastructure cannot be retrofitted and must be part of the initial design. The continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline enforces this, so agents lacking instrumentation fail validation before evaluation runs. We recommend instrumenting three dimensions: Intent tracing: Capture the observable agent trajectory (reasoning steps, tool invocations, and context retrievals) for each execution. OpenTelemetry spans create a queryable lineage from user request to final output. Verification and evaluation as CI: Any change to the agent (prompt edits, tool additions, model swaps) triggers the pipeline. Verification runs first with automated regression tests covering agent components and then their interactions. As most harness components are deterministic, these tests are fast and fully automatable. Evaluation runs second, scoring non-deterministic output against the ground-truth dataset, gated on quality thresholds. This sequencing is deliberate: Verification acts as a gate, so evaluations only run on a passing build. Model tiering and routing telemetry: When agents route between models, capture the routing decision and its justification, not just the outcome. Tier assignments are derived from evaluation results per task type and poor outcomes flow back as new evaluation cases. Start focused, design for composition For distributed cloud systems, the industry solved the complexity of end-to-end workflows by adopting architectural patterns such as microservices or service meshes. The evolution of agentic systems needs to follow a similar trajectory, moving from monolithic, generalist agents toward multiple collaborating specialized agents. Teams should define the problem before considering agents’ functionality. Before writing any orchestration logic, they should produce five concrete artifacts: Clear scope definition: what the agent should and shouldn’t do. Interaction model: how users and other agents will invoke it. Unambiguous tool definitions: each tool and parameter precisely defined. Ground-truth dataset: the evaluation reference described above, established before any implementation begins. Evaluation criteria: quality thresholds and benchmarks the agent will be measured against. This discipline prevents the most common failure modes we observe: agents that take on too many responsibilities accumulate bloated prompts, reducing accuracy and increasing latency. Once a single agent is well-scoped, it must be designed as a composable building block. Therefore, we define a three-tier composition hierarchy: MCP tools are atomic integration contracts. Each tool wraps a single capability (for example, an API call or a database query) without encoding workflow assumptions. This is the stable, reusable layer. Skills are bundled, domain-specific compositions of MCP tools. A code review skill, for example, might chain a static analysis tool, a style-check tool, and an LLM-based reasoning step. Skills encode domain logic but remain portable across workflows. Flows are end-to-end orchestrations of skills, representing complete business processes (for example, an entire PR review pipeline or a requirements-to-deployment cycle). Each tier is validated independently in the CI/CD pipeline. Component tests cover tools and skills, interaction tests cover their composition into flows. These tiers are connected through open standards: MCP and Agent Skills for tool integration, the protocol for agent-to-agent communication, and OpenTelemetry for observability across the resulting interactions. Figure 1 shows how the three tiers build on each other, from individual MCP tools at the base to complete flows at the top. Figure 1: Three-tier system to build composable agents Specialize as you learn In production, even well-scoped agents can break down as real-world usage diverges from what was anticipated at design time: query patterns shift, tool-selection logic struggles, and performance degrades unpredictably. The right response is to decompose complex agents into multiple specialized ones, each with clearer instructions, simpler tool sets, and more focused reasoning. The benefits are concrete: Evolve independently: updating a requirements engineering agent does not require touching the coding agent. Scale individually: when scope and interfaces are well-defined, individual agents can be scaled independently without redeploying or resizing the broader system. Minimized scope: a failure or hallucination of one agent does not cascade across the entire workflow. Cost savings: A narrowly scoped agent can often run on a smaller model, which cuts inference and hosting costs. Complexity can be reduced along two axes: Within an agent: decompose capabilities into skills since tools and few-shot examples consume context on every invocation while degrading accuracy and increasing cost. Determine granularity empirically: merge skills the agent rarely selects and split skills that produce different behavior depending on the input. Across agents: delegate work outside an agent’s domain to a specialized peer over the A2A protocol rather than extending the current agent. An agent should grow in capability, not in context. Critically, since each specialized agent only accesses the data and tools required for its role, this architecture helps to enforce least-privilege by design, a compliance requirement in regulated industries. Realizing these benefits, however, requires that agents can find and interoperate with each other. To prevent the emergence of AI islands, we maintain a centralized registry of agents, tools, and skills. This registry serves as: Discovery mechanism: cataloging available agents, tools, and skills based on metadata stored during build. Governance checkpoint: confirming approval of the asset types for production use and maintaining an audit trail. Security checkpoint: automated security checks are applied before approval, such as prompt injection and similar issues. Deduplication safeguard: identifying equivalent capabilities already maintained by other teams to avoid duplicate work. This check runs automatically at registration, flagging duplicates before approval. Scale through codification The shift from managing individual agents to governing an agent fleet requires agent architectures to be codified. Using Infrastructure-as-code frameworks such as Terraform or AWS CloudFormation, teams provision and manage agent infrastructure with the same rigor applied to any production system: Fine-grained least-privilege roles: scoped per agent or tool. CI/CD pipelines: consistent, validated deployments across accounts and regions, with automated deployment stops on failed tests or metric deterioration. Policy-as-code: rules (for example, AWS Config, Open Policy Agent) scanning deployed agents for compliance with organizational standards. All three are enforced as pipeline gates, validated before registration, not audited after the fact. The adoption model is deliberately bottom-up with central curation. Individual teams build skills and MCP tools to solve their immediate problems. All teams can contribute by sharing their assets through the registry. A central team builds automatic governance checks as part of the CI pipeline to uphold standards. To support development teams and foster shift-left, the central team additionally provides building blocks as governance-as-code modules. This balance avoids both centrally mandated architectures and unmanaged experimentation. As a result, when new operational concerns arise, teams can extend existing patterns rather than redesign their architectures. Operationalizing best practices across the agent lifecycle Architectural patterns and governance standards are only effective if they are embedded into the workflows teams use to build and operate agents before and at runtime. Before deployment Governance begins before a single line of orchestration logic is written. Teams are provided with reference architecture patterns and examples drawn from the registry. These pre-validated blueprints cover common agent configurations, tool integration patterns, and composition structures, which accelerate development while encoding proven defaults. Before anything reaches production, standardized CI/CD controls enforce these practices. Figure 2 shows the four phases of a reference pipeline, which run in order from left to right. Figure 2: Reference pattern for a four-phase agent deployment pipeline. Phase 1 from Figure 2 runs fast, deterministic checks: supply chain security (approved registries only), component and interaction testing, evaluation library references, and observability instrumentation. Phase 2 runs security and governance checks in parallel. Static analysis scans the code for issues, and security tests probe the agent in an isolated staging environment. The pipeline also validates egress controls and least-privilege permissions. Two more checks confirm that the agent’s declared autonomy level matches its actual permissions and that its configuration passes the policy-as-code rules. A governance agent accelerates audits by checking the agent against established standards and flagging findings for human review, such as: Scope creep: operating beyond originally defined purpose or permissions. Prompt bloat: unnecessary complexity in instructions. Tool misuse: calling tools outside their intended use case. Performance degradation: declining accuracy, latency, or cost-efficiency. Figure 3: Example governance agent workflow This assessment surfaces concrete, actionable measures that teams can apply immediately, rather than abstract recommendations. Figure 3 shows the governance agent’s dashboard for an agent maturity assessment. The governance agent provides evidence and actionable recommendations, while accountable humans own governance decisions. Recommendations require human confirmation before being applied, maintaining a four-eyes principle for accountability. Findings update the agent’s governance status in the registry, while full details are logged separately in a central knowledge base for audit and traceability. Phase 3 evaluates the agent as a running system: the ground-truth evaluation gate (scores outputs against benchmarks established at design time) and agent performance (latency, token consumption). Figure 4 details the metrics, scoring criteria and the relationships between them. Figure 4: Overview of evaluation metrics Phase 4 checks for duplicates before registering the agent, its sub-agents, tools, and skills. The following table shows the metadata fields stored per agent in the registry. Agent metadata Core data: unique identifier name description version business owner IT owner Capabilities: names, descriptions Functions list: name, description, direction: provides/ uses Status: plan / active / deprecated Link to specification, agent card or documentation Hosting mode: on-prem, cloud, cloud-region Service level agreement data: Target availability in percent Target P95 response time in ms Support hours / operational support model Data governance flags: information classification level personal data processed flag data retention period/ policy request and response payloads logged flag PII data redacted flag Human in the loop required flag (required for high-impact / irreversible actions) Table 1: Example agent metadata stored in the registry If any step fails or metrics deteriorate, the deployment stops with logs for root cause analysis. If all checks pass, the agent is packaged and deployed as a containerized workload, producing consistent, reproducible deployments. This prevents ungoverned agents from reaching production, automates compliance checks, and keeps the registry accurate. At runtime At runtime, observability has to catch two kinds of drift. Data drift shows up as new or shifting user query patterns, or changes in upstream APIs. Model drift shows as rising error rates or falling tool-selection accuracy. When a customer flags a response, that also triggers an investigation. Alerts for drift, distribution shifts, declining evaluation scores, or direct customer flags prompt a staged response. These events are logged and forwarded to human review. Additionally, teams can run the governance agent continuously to flag drift and operational issues for the responsible team to investigate. Summary Building and operating agents at scale is an engineering discipline, not an experimentation exercise. Effective governance must be structural from the start, externalized, domain-sensitive, and deterministically enforced. We introduced a three-tier composition hierarchy (MCP tools, skills, and flows) as the architectural foundation for reusable, composable, and interoperable agents, decomposed into specialized agents to contain complexity and scope. We showed how verification and evaluation in every CI/CD run make quality assurance part of everyday development, and how defining agent infrastructure as code lets teams apply the same governance rules to every agent in the fleet. Finally, we operationalized these patterns across the agent lifecycle, from pre-validated reference architectures and structured pipelines to a runtime governance agent that continuously evaluates deployed agents. Our experience has shown these practices pay off in a few ways. Reusable templates and shared infrastructure reduced development costs. Teams also got agents to production faster, thanks to standard interaction models and automated deployment. Quality improved too, because the pipeline enforces proven patterns at every stage of the lifecycle. Scaling agentic governance is an industry-wide imperative. The shift toward AI and generative-AI-supported workflow automation is already reshaping how engineering organizations operate. The winners will be those who move beyond experimentation and establish the discipline to govern autonomous agent networks at scale. With these practices in place, BMW engineers can focus on solving the problems that matter: Building the ultimate driving machine. To apply these ideas to your own agents, start with the AWS Well-Architected Framework. This post used it as the model for reusable agent blueprints. To see how BMW codifies governance across its AWS environment, read How BMW Group uses automation to achieve end-to-end compliance at scale on AWS. Outlook and next steps The patterns and practices described in this post are a foundation, not a finish line. We are actively extending them across several fronts: Improve architectural guidance: publishing best practice guides on architectural trade-offs, composition patterns, and anti-patterns for teams building agents. Expand infrastructure-as-code templates: providing agent blueprints as usable IaC modules with built-in security and governance standards by default. Deepen governance compliance testing: adding CI/CD test cases verifying governance compliance. Automate standards enforcement: expanding automated checks and managed compliance-scanning rules across pre-deployment and runtime stages. Extend agentic FinOps: Govern the right-sizing of models and tool calls. Agentic user guidance: integrating described patterns into Archimedes, BMW’s architectural guidance agent, to provide contextual architectural recommendations. items.title: Inside Amazon Connect Talent: The science of structured AI interviews
items.summary: For organizations hiring hundreds or thousands of people, every interview presents the same challenge: How do you give candidates a consistent opportunity to demonstrate their skills while gathering the evidence needed to make informed hiring decisions? Structured behavioral interviews offer a research-backed approach to this challenge. They use consistent, job-related questions and clear scoring criteria to give candidates an opportunity to demonstrate their skills. Decades of research in industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology have shown that structured interviews help organizations evaluate candidates and predict job performance (Schmidt & Hunter, 1998; Sackett et al., 2022). Yet delivering structured interviews at scale requires significant time and expertise to develop competencies, create questions, train interviewers, and evaluate responses consistently. Amazon Connect Talent brings established hiring science to AI-led interviews at scale. Connect Talent uses structured questions, adaptive follow-ups, and evidence-based scoring to help organizations gather consistent, job-related information while giving more candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their strengths. We built Connect Talent around three core design principles and evaluated how well the service applies them through a combination of internal research and independent expert review. The findings offer a closer look at the science behind Connect Talent’s AI-led, structured interviewing. Three core design principles 1. Build interviews around job-related evidence Connect Talent builds each interview around the competencies required for the role. The service uses job requirements and established occupational frameworks to create behaviorally anchored scorecards. Each scorecard defines specific strength and concern signals, and every interview question targets the behaviors it aims to uncover. The AI interviewer also adapts to each response. After every answer, it checks whether the candidate has provided enough evidence for the competency being assessed. When details are missing, it asks targeted follow-up questions. This approach preserves the structure of the interview while giving candidates more opportunities to explain their experience. 2. Separate interviewing from scoring Connect Talent separates the interview conversation from the evaluation. The AI interviewer gathers evidence but does not assign scores. Afterward, a separate evaluation process identifies which behaviors the candidate demonstrated and cites the supporting transcript passages. The service calculates each competency score from 1 to 5 using a fixed formula. When the transcript lacks sufficient evidence, Connect Talent flags the competency instead of producing a score. Hiring teams can review the evidence behind each rating, and missing evidence does not automatically count against the candidate. 3. Build fairness protections into the design Connect Talent evaluates transcribed candidate responses without using video, voice tone, or physical appearance to calculate competency scores. The service also excludes candidate identity information from scoring and evaluates each competency separately. These safeguards help focus assessments on job-related behaviors and limit the influence of unrelated information. What the research shows To understand how well these design principles work in practice, we combined independent I-O psychology evaluations with internal research. We examined whether the service generates job-relevant interview content, identifies behavioral evidence in line with expert assessments, gathers more complete responses through follow-up questions, and distinguishes between levels of demonstrated competency. Connect Talent keeps interview questions focused on job-relevant skills The quality of a structured interview starts with the skills it measures. Candidates need questions that reflect the requirements of the role, and hiring teams need confidence that the interview assesses those skills. Amazon engaged an independent I-O psychology firm to evaluate Connect Talent’s AI-generated interview content. The firm reviewed the service’s baseline output before human editing and examined how well its competencies, questions, and rubrics aligned with job requirements. The evaluation found that Connect Talent retained critical job information in 100% of the job descriptions reviewed. Of the competencies generated, 91% were clearly traceable to the job description. The firm’s psychologists also found that 98% of interview questions targeted the intended competencies, and 94% of rubric signals clearly measured the intended competency. These findings show that Connect Talent generated job-relevant interview content that met independent expert criteria in a vast majority of cases. Hiring teams can then review, select, and edit the competencies, scorecards, and questions before using them. This human oversight gives organizations control over the interview process while helping them apply structured hiring practices at scale. Connect Talent’s candidate scoring matched independent expert decisions more than 89% of the time Relevant questions provide the foundation for a structured interview. The next challenge is evaluating the evidence candidates provide with consistency. To examine this, an independent I-O psychology firm reviewed 36 interviews assessing whether candidates demonstrated specific strengths and concerns, creating 252 rubric signals. Connect Talent evaluated the same transcripts, reviewed hundreds of rubric signals, and aligned with expert scoring decisions in 89.3% of cases. Scoring alignment reached 97.6% when candidates provided clear evidence and 92.9% when only considering candidate concern signals, which identify behaviors that may indicate a poor fit for the intended role. The evaluation also produced a Cohen’s kappa of 0.79, a statistical measure that eliminates random chance coincidence. A Cohen’s kappa of 0.79 is just under the standard of 0.81 for almost perfect agreement. This outcome indicates substantial agreement between Connect Talent and the independent expert candidate scoring. Follow-up questions give candidates more opportunities to demonstrate their strengths Candidates may have relevant experience but leave important details out of their first response. In a traditional one-way video interview, a candidate may receive a fixed question and have only one opportunity to answer it. Hiring teams must then evaluate the information available, even when the response leaves many important questions unanswered. Connect Talent uses adaptive follow-ups to gather more complete evidence. For example, a candidate might describe improving a slow system. The AI interviewer can ask what changed, which actions the candidate took, and how they measured the improvement. These questions help candidates explain their contributions and results in greater detail. We studied the impact of follow-up questions by comparing assessments based on a candidate’s first response with assessments based on the full interview conversation. In a preliminary evaluation, scores based only on the first response were up to 1.14 points lower on a five-point scale than scores based on the full conversation. Assessments using the full conversation also came closer to expert evaluations. Without follow-up questions, the scoring process identified fewer strength signals and more concern signals. In some cases, the candidate’s initial response simply lacked the information needed to demonstrate a relevant behavior. The full conversation captured more of what candidates demonstrated and gave hiring teams a more complete record of their experience. Structured scoring helps hiring teams recognize meaningful differences Hiring teams need scores that reflect meaningful differences in demonstrated skills. Yet research has found that some AI scoring approaches concentrate ratings within a narrow range, making those differences harder to recognize (Zhu et al., 2026). Connect Talent uses behaviorally anchored scorecards to evaluate specific strength and concern signals. Rather than asking an AI model to assign an overall rating, the service identifies evidence for each behavior and calculates the competency score using a predefined formula. Consider the competency “collaboration”. A general AI scoring approach might evaluate a candidate’s overall collaboration skills based on the interview transcript. Connect Talent examines specific behaviors, such as whether the candidate sought input from colleagues before making a decision. Each finding contributes to the final score. We evaluated this approach across hundreds of expert-rated interview assessments. Connect Talent’s structured scoring used all five points of the rating scale, while holistic LLM-as-judge scoring concentrated its ratings within the middle three points. This wider distribution allows the scoring system to represent more levels of demonstrated competency. The behaviorally anchored scorecards also help hiring teams understand the evidence behind each rating. Bringing hiring science to AI-led interviews Connect Talent brings the rigor of structured interviewing to more people while giving each candidate a meaningful chance to demonstrate their skills. The result is a new opportunity for organizations hiring at scale: more candidates can show what they can do, and more hiring teams can make decisions grounded in the evidence that matters. The session will explore the science behind Connect Talent, including structured interviewing, adaptive follow-up questions, and evidence-based scoring. Earlier, he completed a PhD in information at the University of Michigan and a postdoc at Georgia Tech, where he researched how to evaluate large language models on social factors. His specialties include large language model evaluation, natural language processing, and structured interview design.​
