items.title: Keep inference running through regional capacity shortfalls with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
items.summary: Serving a model from more than one AWS Region is a well-established pattern for highly available inference: when one Region runs short of GPU capacity, requests move to another. The pattern is simple to describe and hard to operate. Until now, if you served models on Amazon SageMaker AI managed endpoints, cross-Region routing was a piece you still had to build yourself. Today, we’re introducing cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. It uses a new resource, the inference router, that gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in one or more AWS Regions and AWS accounts. You register the destinations that serve a model, and your application invokes the router instead of a specific endpoint. The router keeps requests in its own Region while the local destination is healthy, shifts new requests to another registered destination when it isn’t, and returns traffic gradually after recovery. In this post, we explain how cross-Region inference routing decides where each request runs, walk through an example with one model in two Regions, and cover monitoring, limits, and what you pay. For a cross-account deployment that serves several models, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. When one Region runs short of capacity A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in one AWS Region and one account. When autoscaling can’t add instances of the type your endpoint needs, requests throttle and time out, even when the same model has spare capacity in another Region. To use that capacity, your application must detect a struggling endpoint and switch Regions, decide which errors are safe to retry without running the model twice, move traffic back after recovery without flapping, and manage access to endpoints in other accounts. That code sits on the critical path of every request, and every team serving models across Regions maintains its own version of it. How cross-Region inference routing works Cross-Region inference routing is based on a few core ideas: You decide where your model might run – For each model, you choose which endpoints and inference components the router might use. SageMaker AI decides which destination serves each request – The router prefers its own Region and shifts new requests to another destination only when the local one can’t serve reliably. Your endpoints stay the same – You deploy endpoints as you do today, with the same models, configurations, instance pools, and autoscaling. Direct InvokeEndpoint calls keep working, and the router passes InferenceId and CustomAttributes through, as InvokeEndpoint does. You can see every decision – Each real-time response tells you which destination served the request and why. A few terms describe the pieces: Inference router – A Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account that your application invokes. Routing target – A name for one logical model on a router, such as fraud-model. A router can hold many routing targets, and each fails over independently of the others. Destination – A real-time endpoint, inference component, or asynchronous endpoint registered under a routing target, identified by its full Amazon Resource Name (ARN), which tells the router its Region and account. A routing target holds either real-time destinations, which can mix endpoints and inference components across Regions and accounts, or asynchronous endpoints only. Local destination – A destination in the router’s Region, preferred while it’s healthy. Routing reason – A value returned with each real-time response that explains where the request went and why. The Region you create the router in is its local Region. To prefer a different Region, create a router there. The router doesn’t create capacity, scale your endpoints, deploy models, or copy model artifacts and container images. Each destination must already be running in its Region. Figure 1: Each request goes to a healthy destination, with the router preferring destinations in its own Region How routing decisions are made The router considers only destinations that are registered on the routing target and that it’s authorized to invoke. Among those, it prefers destinations in its own Region, and when more than one local destination is healthy, it spreads requests across them evenly. Requests leave the Region only when local destinations can’t serve reliably. To detect that, SageMaker AI calculates a health score for each destination from its recent requests, measured in the destination’s own Region. Server errors (5xx), throttles, and timeouts lower the score. Errors from the SageMaker AI platform (for example, failed health check) lower it the most. Errors caused by the request itself, such as invalid input, don’t lower it, because the same request would fail in any Region. Model latency isn’t an input, so an endpoint that keeps returning successful responses keeps its traffic. Signals such as failed instance launches or an endpoint running fewer instances than its autoscaling target make the router react faster, but only after the destination starts failing requests. The router evaluates each destination’s health and publishes it to Amazon CloudWatch as one of three states. A healthy destination serves normally. An overloaded destination still serves, and the router moves part of its traffic away. A degraded destination is failing or can’t serve, so the router moves most of its traffic away and keeps a small share to detect recovery. Figure 2: How each destination health state changes the traffic the router sends to it SageMaker AI manages failover thresholds and timing, so you don’t need to tune any thresholds. If health information for remote destinations goes stale, the router keeps traffic in its own Region, so a gap in monitoring never moves traffic on its own. When traffic moves, and when it comes back The more requests fail, the more traffic moves, so a destination need not fail outright first. Traffic starts to move within about a minute of sustained errors, or longer for a destination with little traffic. Traffic that leaves the local Region is spread across the healthy remote destinations in proportion to their health. You can’t set weights or a fallback order. After recovery, traffic returns over several minutes, more slowly than it left. Requests in progress aren’t interrupted. When a destination fails a real-time request without running the model, the router retries that request once on a different destination. This covers, for example, a throttle, a 503 error, a model that isn’t ready, a rejection by a cross-Region traffic cap, or access denied by the destination. The router never retries timeouts, 500 errors, or model errors. For asynchronous requests, the router tries each eligible destination once, local destinations first, until one accepts the request. Figure 3: The router retries a real-time request once on another destination, and only when the model didn’t run Figure 4 shows where requests were served in one of our tests with a test model. Figure 4: Where requests were served as the local endpoint was overloaded, a destination in another account lost and regained access, and the local endpoint recovered What you can route The following use cases show common ways to use cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. Keep serving when one Region runs short of GPU capacity. When your G-series instance type runs short in US East (Ohio) during peak traffic and requests start to throttle, the router shifts new requests to the same model in US West (Oregon), where autoscaling absorbs the overflow, and moves traffic back gradually after US East (Ohio) recovers. Route across endpoints owned by separate AWS accounts. When a central platform account owns the router and other accounts own the endpoints, each endpoint owner grants access to one named router, and requests reach those endpoints only through that router. We cover the setup after this list. Serve many models from one router. Create one router with one routing target per model, each listing that model’s destinations, and pass the routing target name on each request. Each model fails over independently. Put the router behind your own gateway. If you operate an API or model gateway, you can point its SageMaker AI integration at the router, so SageMaker AI handles Region selection for SageMaker-hosted models while your gateway decides when to use a different provider. For example, see the Salesforce post. Route asynchronous requests. Asynchronous endpoints, in the router’s account or in other accounts, can be destinations. Your application calls InvokeInferenceRouterAsync with the routing target name and the Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) input location, and gets back an InferenceId and the output and failure locations, as with InvokeEndpointAsync. Protect a receiving endpoint from other Regions’ overflow. On a real-time endpoint, you can set an optional cross-Region traffic cap so that requests from other Regions can use only part of its capacity. Your endpoint’s local callers keep the rest. We cover the details later in this section. When a destination belongs to a different account than the router, both accounts must allow each request. On the endpoint side, the owner attaches a resource-based policy that allows the router account to invoke the endpoint, and the sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn condition key limits that access to one named router. The following policy allows only my-router in account 444455556666 to invoke the endpoint. Its second statement has no router condition and lets the router account read the endpoint’s status. Without that statement, the destination shows its status as unknown. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowOneRouter", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:root"}, "Action": ["sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint", "sagemaker:InvokeEndpointAsync"], "Resource": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:111122223333:endpoint/my-endpoint", "Condition": {"ArnEquals": { "sagemaker:SourceInferenceRouterArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-2:444455556666:inference-router/my-router"}} }, { "Sid": "AllowStatusVisibility", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::444455556666:root"}, "Action": "sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint", "Resource": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:111122223333:endpoint/my-endpoint" } ] } In the router account, callers need sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouter (or sagemaker:InvokeInferenceRouterAsync) on the router and sagemaker:InvokeEndpoint (or sagemaker:InvokeEndpointAsync) on every destination, because the router invokes each destination on the caller’s behalf. A router never gives a caller access to an endpoint they couldn’t call directly. For DescribeInferenceRouter to report each destination’s status, callers also need sagemaker:DescribeEndpoint on endpoints and sagemaker:DescribeInferenceComponent on inference components. Applications in other accounts call the router by assuming a role in the router account. For a walkthrough, see How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI and User Guide on cross-account destinations. Figure 5: Controls the endpoint owner keeps: an endpoint policy that allows one named router, and an optional cross-Region traffic cap Protect a receiving endpoint with a cross-Region traffic cap When the router moves requests away from a Region that’s short on capacity, those requests land on endpoints that already serve their own Region’s callers. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so a surge of overflow can push it into throttling. With a cross-Region traffic cap, the endpoint owner decides how much of the endpoint’s capacity other Regions might use. You set the cap in CreateEndpointConfig with CrossRegionTrafficConfig, which takes two required values. MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance is the number of invocations per second that one instance can take, which you measure with a load test of your model, instance type, and typical payload. MaxCrossRegionPercentPerEndpoint is the share of that capacity that other Regions might use. SageMaker AI multiplies the per-instance rate by the instances in service and applies the percentage, so the cap follows autoscaling. For example, with 50 invocations per second per instance, a 20 percent cap, and 4 instances in service, the endpoint accepts up to 40 requests per second from other Regions. When autoscaling adds 2 instances, the cap rises to 60 requests per second. sm = boto3.client("sagemaker", region_name="us-west-2") sm.create_endpoint_config( EndpointConfigName="my-model-config-us-west-2", ProductionVariants=[...], # your existing variants, unchanged CrossRegionTrafficConfig={ "MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance": 50, "MaxCrossRegionPercentPerEndpoint": 20, }, ) Only requests from other Regions count against the cap. Requests from the endpoint’s own Region, including direct InvokeEndpoint calls and calls from a router in the same Region, are never throttled by it. When cross-Region requests exceed the cap, the endpoint rejects the extra requests before your model runs, and the router retries each one once on a different destination. If no other destination can take the request, your application gets a throttling error. The cap applies to real-time endpoints, and all inference components on an endpoint share it. For an endpoint that hosts inference components, load test one instance with its usual mix of inference components and payloads to measure MaxInvocationsPerSecondPerInstance, and run the test again when that mix or your payloads change. If you leave out CrossRegionTrafficConfig, the endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic. Get started: One model in two Regions In this example, we deploy Qwen3-4B with the vLLM container as an inference component in US East (Ohio) and US West (Oregon), in one account. Because the inference router doesn’t support response streaming, the application sends non-streaming requests, and each request must complete within about a minute, the same limit as InvokeEndpoint. We then create a router in US East (Ohio) with one routing target that lists both: sm = boto3.client("sagemaker", region_name="us-east-2") rt = boto3.client("sagemaker-inference-router-runtime", region_name="us-east-2") sm.create_inference_router( InferenceRouterName="my-router", RoutingTargets=[{ "Name": "my-model", "Destinations": [ {"ResourceArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-east-2:111122223333:inference-component/ic-us-east-2"}, {"ResourceArn": "arn:aws:sagemaker:us-west-2:111122223333:inference-component/ic-us-west-2"}, ], }], ) Run DescribeInferenceRouter and confirm that each destination’s RoutingStatus is Routable before you send traffic. The application invokes the router with the routing target name and the same payload it would send to InvokeEndpoint, and reads the serving destination and routing reason from the response: resp = rt.invoke_inference_router( InferenceRouterName="my-router", RoutingTargetName="my-model", ContentType="application/json", Body=json.dumps({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Who are you?"}]}), ) print("Served by:", resp["InvokedRoutedResourceArn"]) print("Reason: ", resp["RoutingReason"]) What we observed Step RoutingStatus in DescribeInferenceRouter (us-east-2 / us-west-2) Served by Routing reason Both inference components running Routable / Routable us-east-2 local-preferred us-east-2 inference component removed Unroutable / Routable us-west-2 only-healthy us-east-2 inference component restored Routable / Routable us-west-2 only-healthy Traffic back in us-east-2 Routable / Routable us-east-2 local-preferred Traffic stayed in US East (Ohio) while its inference component ran, moved to US West (Oregon) with no change to the application when we removed it, and came back after we restored it. The complete notebook for this example is available on GitHub. Tip: Use instance pools and cross-Region inference routing together. With a capacity-aware instance pool, SageMaker AI can use another instance type in the same Region at creation and during scale-out. The router moves new requests to another Region when the local endpoint as a whole can’t serve. For details, see Capacity-aware inference: Automatic instance fallback for SageMaker AI endpoints. See where each request went The inference router gives you two views of routing: a record on every real-time response and metrics in CloudWatch. Per-request routing record Every real-time response includes the ARN of the destination that served the request in InvokedRoutedResourceArn, and the routing reason in RoutingReason. The routing reason is one of the following: local-preferred – Served by a healthy destination in the router’s Region. capacity-available – Served by a destination with available capacity. failover – Moved away from a destination that couldn’t serve reliably. only-healthy – Served by the only eligible destination that was healthy. We recommend logging both values with your application’s own request logs. Asynchronous responses don’t include the serving destination. Router metrics in CloudWatch show where asynchronous requests were placed. Router metrics in CloudWatch The router publishes OpenTelemetry metrics to CloudWatch in its own account and Region, labeled with the router, routing target, and destination: aws.sagemaker.inference_router.invocations – Requests per destination, with an error.type label on failures (invocation_4xx, invocation_5xx, or invocation_model_error). aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.duration – Time at the destination, including your model. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.overhead.duration – The router’s own work plus network time to and from another Region. aws.sagemaker.inference_router.destination.status – Each destination as healthy, overloaded, or degraded. Alarm on destinations that aren’t healthy and on the error rate across all error types. See Monitor an inference routers with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail. Figure 6: Requests per destination from the router’s CloudWatch invocations metric during the test shown in Figure 4 Each destination endpoint keeps publishing its existing SageMaker AI metrics in its own account and Region. To view them in one place, use CloudWatch cross-account observability and cross-account cross-Region dashboards. AWS CloudTrail records the router’s API calls (create, update, delete, describe, and list) as management events and router invocations as data events. You enable data events on your trail as you do for other SageMaker AI data events. Plan your deployment Keep the following in mind when you design with the inference router: Put the router in the Region where most of your traffic originates. The router always prefers destinations in its own Region. Size each Region for its own traffic plus the overflow you want it to absorb. By default, a receiving endpoint accepts any amount of cross-Region traffic, so configure autoscaling with headroom for the overflow you expect. To protect an endpoint’s local callers, set a cross-Region traffic cap, as described in Protect a receiving endpoint with a cross-Region traffic cap. If every remote destination reaches its cap, requests beyond the combined caps return throttling errors. Keep a low-cost standby Region. You can register an inference component in another Region and keep its cost low, but plan for how it gets capacity. A remote inference component with zero copies receives only a small share of traffic during failover, and those requests fail until it has copies. Keep at least one copy running, or configure autoscaling on copies and confirm that it scales out before you rely on the standby Region. Plan for resilience at the entry point. A router is regional, so if its Region is impaired, calls to it fail. Create routers in two Regions and switch between them on the client side. Register only destinations where your data might be processed. A request can be processed in the router’s Region or in any Region where you’ve registered a destination. For data that must stay in one geography, use a separate router, for example one for US data and one for EU data. You are responsible for configuring your routers to align with your data residency and compliance obligations. Keep your own retries modest. A throttling error means every destination was busy, and a service-unavailable error means no destination could take the request. A service-unavailable error after about a minute means the request timed out and the model might have run, so don’t retry it automatically. Remove deleted destinations from the router. Traffic already avoids a deleted endpoint, but the router never removes a destination on its own. Call the router privately. Applications in a virtual private cloud (VPC) can call the router through an interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink), which supports IPv4 (IPv6/dual-stack not supported). Also note the following limitations: Response streaming isn’t supported. A real-time request that the destination doesn’t respond to within about a minute fails with a service-unavailable error. Each router holds up to 20 routing targets, each routing target holds up to 10 destinations, and real-time payloads can be up to 6 MB. For default quotas, such as routers per account and request rates, and how to request an increase, see Service Quotas in the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation. Conclusion Cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI gives your application one invocation path across the endpoints and inference components you already run, in multiple AWS Regions and AWS accounts. The router prefers its own Region, shifts new requests when a destination can’t serve reliably, returns traffic gradually after recovery, and shows you where each request ran and why. Your endpoints, models, containers, and autoscaling policies don’t change. Cross-Region inference routing is generally available starting today in most commercial AWS Regions (except me-south-1 and me-central-1), for real-time and asynchronous inference. There is no additional charge for cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI. You pay for the SageMaker AI endpoints and inference components that serve your requests at standard SageMaker AI pricing, whether a request reaches them directly or through an inference router. The inference router publishes metrics to Amazon CloudWatch in the router’s account, and you pay standard CloudWatch rates for those metrics and any queries you run on them. For details, see Amazon SageMaker AI pricing. To get started, see the Amazon SageMaker AI documentation on cross-Region inference routing and explore the sample notebook on GitHub. About the authors Dmitry Soldatkin Dmitry is a Worldwide Leader for Specialist Solutions Architecture, Amazon SageMaker AI Inference at AWS. He helps customers design, build, and optimize generative AI and machine learning solutions, with a focus on inference performance optimization, deep learning, and scaling ML across the enterprise. In previous roles, he led teams at financial services, insurance, and telecommunications companies. Apoorva Chandra Apoorva is a Product Manager on the Amazon SageMaker AI Inference team, where she focuses on the endpoint experience and hosting experience. She works with customers deploying generative AI models in production to make accelerated compute easier to obtain, more cost-efficient to run, and more predictable to operate. Outside of work, Apoorva enjoys hiking, exploring coffee shops, and spending time with friends. Deepti Ragha Deepti is a Senior Software Development Engineer on the Amazon SageMaker AI team, specializing in ML inference infrastructure and model hosting optimization. She builds features that improve deployment performance, availability and reduce inference costs, and make ML accessible to organizations of all sizes. Outside of work, she enjoys traveling, hiking, and gardening. Felipe Lopez Felipe is a Principal AI/ML Specialist Solutions Architect at AWS. Prior to joining AWS, Felipe worked with GE Digital and SLB, where he focused on modeling and optimization products for industrial applications. Barkha Saxena Barkha is a Software Development Engineer at Amazon SageMaker AI Inference team, specializing in ML inference infrastructure and model serving optimization. Her work spans efficient multi-adapter inference, which serves hundreds of fine-tuned LoRA adapters from a single endpoint, and bidirectional streaming for low-latency, real-time applications such as voice agents. Outside work, she enjoys table tennis, painting, and puzzles.

items.title: OpenViking 3D 理解模型 X 汽车行业 Benchmark 数据库
items.summary: 原创 OpenViking 2026-11-19 18:00 北京 OpenViking如何理解整车数据 OpenViking 10月20日发布原生3D内容理解模型，支持三维.STEP, .DWG文件的导入与解析，信息还原率做到 100%。以如下整车模型为例，包含174个零件定义，445个安装实例。 导入整车模型，OpenViking首先会围绕零部件、装配关系进行拆解，形成【整车概览-车身-底盘-动力总成-内饰-仪表盘与中控-外饰-座椅-电子电器-空调-流体】的结构目录。 原始模型 整车模型结构目录 再基于3D理解模型，将零件拆分归类，分别解析出其中的几何、尺寸、公差、工艺数据，并保留完整的装配关系。 解析目录 正交六视图 轴侧八视图 信息摘要（含PMI） 模型明细 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 以上内容，OpenViking 均会建立索引，并用于下游模型推理。接入 Agent 后，可以在以下场景感受到价值。 场景一｜一句话找到设计参考 一位底盘工程师要做前置后驱跑车的后悬架，想参考捷豹 E-Type。 以前，你要在库里逐层翻目录，从底盘一路找到动力总成，再打开 3D 模型区分前后零件，半天才能整理出一张表。 现在，只需要将模型库、项目资料、采购清单上传到OpenViking，连接到你使用的 Agent。 对它说：“参考捷豹 E-Type 的后悬架，列出零件、材料和重量，说说布置特点，再估一下总重和成本”。 Agent 会跨目录找齐零件，按装配位置排除前悬架，还能看出每侧两套弹簧减振器的经典设计，最后给出清单：后悬架约 73 kg，加入差速器和半轴后为95.71kg，共29个零件和49个安装实例。 OpenViking + Codex检索 检索到的库内模型 模型信息摘要（含PMI） 生成的BOM清单及成本估算 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 甚至，当你说不出名字，Agent也能通过特征，帮你找到那个零件。例如：“发动机舱里那个装液体的塑料罐子是什么材料”。 OpenViking + Codex检索 检索到的库内模型 模型信息摘要中的关键信息 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 以后，产品怎么设计、用什么材料、有多重，一句话就能拿到参考。 场景二｜设计完快速估算成本 一位动力总成工程师刚完成变速箱方案，但他并不知道设计的零件、系统，成本是多少。汽车行业卷成本，但最懂设计的人却无法进行成本估算。 现在，只需要将历史的BOM清单、采购记录上传到OpenViking，连接到你使用的Agent。 对它说：“统计这台车变速箱的零件，按材料汇总重量，结合库里的单价和费率估一下成本，列出最贵的 5 个零件”。 Agent 会自动按公司的计价口径逐件核算，并给到结论：共统计出 42 种零件、99 件，净重合计 48kg。总成本为 2,348.61 元/套，含 12% 管理及利润。零件已按单价直接成本排序。 以后，工程师不仅专注设计，也能兼顾成本，甚至做到初步的采购，交付速度更快、采购成本更低。 OpenViking + Codex检索 定位到的目录 所有相关零件 生成的BOM清单及成本估算 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 场景三｜标准件归并，降低成本 一位成本工程师在为新车型找降本空间。整车有几十种紧固件，同一个规格混用了好几套标准，零件号越积越多，采购和库存成本也跟着上涨。但要逐个比对规格、标准和使用位置，人工几乎做不完。 现在，只需要将公司的紧固件目录、归并原则、采购单价上传到 OpenViking，连接到你使用的 Agent。 对它说：“整车的标准紧固件用了多少种规格？找出规格相同、标准不同的螺栓，给出可以合并的建议”。 Agent 会读取每个紧固件的名称和 3D 几何，名称里没写规格的，也能从直径、六角对边和长度推断出来。再按公司规则逐条判断：同为 M8×40 的六角螺栓，澳标件可以直接改成 ISO 标准；细牙件要先确认使用位置；英制螺母需要连同配合件一起替换。最后给出结果：参与分析的 47 种紧固件，直接归并后剩 43 种，待确认项全部通过后可降到 38 种。 以后，标准件归并不用再靠人工逐项比对，一句话就能找到降本空间。 整车解析目录 定位到的零件之一 生成的归并示意图 左右滑动查看更多精彩内容 最后 OpenViking 作为首个原生支持 3D 理解的 Agent 上下文数据库产品，能够帮忙汽车行业快速构建Benchmark数据库，连接 Agent，快速找到设计参考 -> 估算成本 -> 归并降本，大幅缩短交付周期，降本增效。现在接入，点击「阅读原文」，即刻使用。 🚀 上手试用，前 50 文档免费： volcengine.com/product/openviking-service 🌟 开源 OpenViking： 访问 GitHub items.title: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach
items.summary: As enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice shows AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has launched the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline. In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock. Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality. Attribution first: Measuring cost at the business level Before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce. Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports, handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call. Telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste. The six optimization levers The goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact. Phase 1: Configuration only, no infrastructure change With Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching). Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response. Both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires new infrastructure or architecture changes. Phase 2: Architectural changes Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy (see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer. Two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains. Phase 3: Infrastructure and training investment Semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a new request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings (see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that users don’t receive outdated answers. Model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment. In production: Four client engagements Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever. The first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching. Accenture applied three changes together: model tiering to match each task to the smallest model that could handle it well, prompt caching for repeated context, and batch processing for overnight and non-urgent jobs. Together they cut monthly token cost by 85 percent, and the saving was not separated by change. About 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning, and the rest ran on lighter models. Your split will depend on your workload composition. The second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend. Most of that spend came from agents fanning out requests without limits and from every request going to a frontier model regardless of complexity. Accenture applied triage routing, semantic caching, and context compression together. Input tokens fell by 70 percent, and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. Accenture validated output quality against the operator’s pre-change performance benchmarks. The third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer. An insurer used model-layer prefix caching, reusing the static portions of its prompts across invocations. A mining operator used an application-layer semantic cache, returning stored responses for repeated queries before they reached the model. Across the two engagements, token spend fell by about 40 percent combined, without model routing changes or training investment. Results Outcomes ranged from about 40 percent to about 85 percent, reflecting each client’s starting point. The large enterprise deployment began with no optimization in place and reached 85 percent. The telecom operator reached 68 percent on $12 million in annual token spend, and the insurer and mining operator reached about 40 percent combined with one caching lever each. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. These savings aren’t the end goal. They create capacity to scale AI workloads, reinvest in higher-value use cases, and improve the return generated by each dollar of AI consumption. Two of these engagements applied several changes at once. When you apply one lever at a time, you can attribute each result to a specific change. AWS and Accenture recommend this sequence for your own workloads: connect consumption to owners and outcomes, apply one lever at a time, measure cost, quality, and business value, and build on what works. Production governance: Four operating tenets Optimizing AI economics in production requires an ongoing governance cycle spanning cost, quality, risk, and business value, not a one-time technical change. Before you apply any lever, establish a quantitative baseline for both cost and quality so that you can measure the impact of each change against a known starting point. When you validate output quality, use held-out evaluation sets drawn from your actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks. Apply one lever at a time per workload so that you can attribute results to a specific change and roll back cleanly if quality drops below your acceptable thresholds. If you operate in a regulated industry such as financial services, insurance, or healthcare, document your quality test results and rollback procedures as part of your standard change management record. These four tenets apply regardless of which levers you are using or what phase of the sequencing you are in. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an environment where you can build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. It includes AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides batch evaluation to support your quality validation cycle as you progress through more advanced levers. Getting started You can begin with three steps. First, turn on cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock by applying cost allocation tags at the team and workload level so that your spend is traceable from day one. Second, activate those tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Then use CUR 2.0 and model invocation logging to identify high-consumption workloads, and assess each one based on spend, business value, quality requirements, risk, volume, and optimization potential. Third, apply Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to that workload’s interactive traffic and Amazon Bedrock batch inference to its asynchronous jobs as configuration-only changes, and measure the result before you move to architectural changes in Phase 2. The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens includes model invocation and token cost optimization (AGENTCOST02), a focus area within the cost optimization pillar for agentic workloads. This focus area provides a structured framework you can use to apply these levers at scale across your organization. About the authors Ilan Geller Ilan is a Managing Director at Accenture, focused on artificial intelligence, delivery, and client growth. Steven Cox Steven is an Associate Director in the Accenture AWS Business Group and a Principal Architect specializing in AWS. He leads token economics work across Accenture client engagements. Manoj Ravulapati Manoj is a Senior Customer Solutions Manager at AWS who leads strategic AI initiatives, helping enterprises scale agentic AI. Rajdeep Banerjee Rajdeep is a Senior Solutions Architect in the AWS Cloud Center of Excellence. He works with AWS partners to design and optimize generative AI workloads on Amazon Bedrock.

items.title: Run your whole selling business in AWS Quick
items.summary: Most sellers do not need another AI product to learn. They need the tools and information they already use brought together, so they can see what is happening in their business and act on it. AWS Quick and the Amazon Selling Partner plugin do that together. Quick brings an Amazon seller’s sales data, inventory signals, and marketplace intelligence into one place, where questions become answers and answers become actions. It understands the seller’s full business context, so the seller does not need to re-explain their catalog, their margins, or their competitive landscape in every conversation. It is built on AWS, the same infrastructure Amazon uses to run its own marketplace. At Amazon Accelerate on September 23, 2026, Amazon announced the Selling Partner plugin and launched it in beta in AWS Quick. This post covers what launched, how to claim the free AWS Quick offer, and what the experience looks like day to day. It also covers how the skills and connectors work when a seller puts them to use. Limited-time offer: 12 months of AWS Quick Plus, free. Every primary selling account holder worldwide can claim a free 12-month subscription, plus access for 10 additional users you delegate. Sign up by December 31, 2026. Claim your free AWS Quick Plus offer. 1. Why Quick is right for Amazon sellers Four things make Quick a fit for how Amazon sellers already work: it learns the business, it reaches beyond the Amazon store, it turns data into decisions, and it protects seller data on infrastructure sellers already trust. Quick knows your business, not only your prompts Quick and the Selling Partner plugin connect to a seller’s inventory feeds, sales data, and operational documents. From these, Quick builds a living understanding of the catalog structure, margin thresholds, seasonality, and competitive position. Ask Quick to audit your ASINs for Q4, and it returns a ranked recommendation built on the seller’s real margin data, historical conversion, and inventory availability. Its recommendations get sharper the more the seller works with it. Quick does not stop at your Amazon store A seller’s business runs across many tools: a storefront on another channel, an email inbox, an accounting system, spreadsheets, a supplier portal. Quick connects to where the seller already works and pulls context from across the whole operation. It is a business assistant that happens to know Amazon deeply, so the seller grows overall, not on one channel alone. It turns data into decisions you can act on Sellers are not short on data. They have Brand Analytics, Search Query Performance, advertising reports, inventory health, and listing quality data. The problem is turning those signals into one clear action. Quick does the synthesis. It watches for change, flags what matters, builds the analysis, and presents the decision with the evidence behind it. Your data stays protected on the infrastructure you already sell on Quick runs on AWS and does not use seller data to train models, not for general improvement and not for anything else. Seller data stays in the seller’s environment and never informs anyone else’s models. For a seller already operating on the Amazon marketplace, there is no new security posture to evaluate. The infrastructure is the same one protecting the seller account today, and the seller’s chosen AWS Region governs where data stays. The Amazon Selling Partner plugin The Selling Partner plugin connects AWS Quick directly to live Seller Central data. After one sign-in with a Seller Central account, the plugin gives conversational access to product listings, inventory, and sales data, pulled live rather than exported and reassembled by hand. It installs like an app, with no coding required. It ships with curated Amazon skills, and it pairs with Amazon Ads MCP so campaign performance and spend sit next to the selling data. The plugin is in beta for US stores. Figure 1: The Selling Partner plugin consent screen, where the seller grants None, View, or Edit access per data category The permission screen is worth a pause. The seller grants access per data category, choosing None, View, or Edit for each, and reviews an agreement before authorizing. Nothing is all-or-nothing, and access can be narrowed or revoked later. 2. How to redeem the Quick Plus offer Claim your free AWS Quick Plus subscription (12 months free plus 10 delegated users, by December 31, 2026). Connect the Selling Partner plugin with one sign-in to your Seller Central account. It installs like an app. Ask your first question, something you would normally build a spreadsheet for. Figure 2: Connecting the Selling Partner plugin from the AWS Quick sign-up flow 3. What the experience looks like After the plugin is connected, the work happens in a conversation. You ask in plain language, Quick pulls the relevant live data, and it comes back with an answer and a recommended next step. Instead of checking a dashboard, exporting a report, and reconciling it in a spreadsheet, you move from a question to an answer to an action in one place. You review what Quick proposes before anything is sent. Figure 3: Quick diagnosing whether a sales dip comes from traffic or conversion, using live selling data 4. Two use cases a seller can build At the Accelerate workshop we had sellers build real agents live, from a plain-language description, in a few minutes. Quick turns the description into a working agent, which the seller then refines in conversation. Use case A: Inventory Launch Prep The seller is staging a new product into Amazon and wants the lowest total landed cost. The agent reads supplier data and weighs the fulfillment options per SKU on inbound cost, storage, and speed to sellable. It walks through placement choices and returns the output the seller picks: a shipping plan, a cost comparison, or a combined packet. It explains its reasoning and confirms before it creates anything. Figure 4: The Inventory Launch Prep agent comparing FBA and AWD fulfillment per factor and recommending a hybrid approach Use case B: Post-Launch Product Health After the launch, the agent reads four signal families through the Selling Partner plugin: listing health, inventory, sales, and traffic. It connects them to find the cause rather than just reporting numbers. Flat sales with healthy traffic points to a conversion problem. Flat sales with falling traffic points to discoverability. Good conversion with falling units points to supply. It returns a health summary per ASIN, the diagnosis with evidence, and a ranked fix list, labeling any low-confidence call. Figure 5: The Post-Launch Product Health agent’s weekly summary, with week-over-week sales evidence One honest limit, handled honestly: the selling data does not include cost of goods, so the agent reports margin after Amazon fees and labels it that way. When the seller wants true gross margin, the agent asks them to bring their cost numbers into the conversation. It never presents after-fees margin as if it were gross margin. 5. Skills and connectors in action The Selling Partner plugin and Amazon Ads MCP bring the Amazon selling and advertising data into Quick. Other connectors in AWS Quick bring in the rest of how the business runs, organized by role. These include a second storefront (orders and products from another channel), email and calendar (draft a supplier note, track what is due), team messaging (share an update), and accounting and inventory systems (cost and stock context the selling data does not carry). Because the pieces sit together, the seller can ask one question that reaches across Amazon data and the tools around it. 6. A seller’s morning, start to finish At Accelerate, Richard Brown, who runs the sneaker care brand Proof Culture and sells across five stores including Amazon, showed what this looks like. He had built his own AI assistant over time, and the hard part was never the AI. It was getting his selling data connected in real time. “The hard part was never the AI. The hard part was getting my selling data into it, and that is the part that is now simple with the plugin. With Quick and the Selling Partner plugin, just connect your account and start asking questions.” — Richard Brown, Proof Culture, at Amazon Accelerate 2026 In his demo, Richard asked Quick about upcoming sneaker drops and checked whether he had enough FBA stock to cover a major release. He had Quick model how far his current inventory would carry him. Then he asked it to draft a reorder purchase order and a message to his team. A morning of research across different tools took a few minutes. 7. Getting started Claim your free year of AWS Quick Plus (by December 31, 2026). Connect the Selling Partner plugin. Follow the setup instructions to connect the Ads MCP within AWS Quick so you can manage campaigns conversationally alongside your selling data. Connect the rest of your business by role: your other storefront, email and calendar, accounting and inventory systems, team messaging. Start with one real question you would normally handle in a spreadsheet. Next steps: Claim your free year of AWS Quick Plus Learn more about AWS Quick Read the AWS Quick documentation Media captured from the Amazon Accelerate 2026 workshop ‘Build It Live: Automate New Product Launch in AWS Quick.’ Non-Amazon tools referred to by role, not brand. About the authors Josh Anderson Josh is a Senior Worldwide GenAI Solutions Architect for AWS Quick. Josh works with customers large and small to adopt AI solutions that accelerate their growth. Jessica Fung Jessica leads Product Marketing for Selling Partner Agentic Primitives & Interfaces at Amazon. Jessica works on go-to-market strategy and enablement for selling partners. Jessie Nishimiya Jessie is a Product Marketing Manager at Amazon owning GTM strategies for seller AI products. Jessie’s work focuses on bringing AI-powered tools to market that help sellers simplify and automate how they manage and grow their businesses. Weiling Gu Weiling is a Senior Solutions Architect for Selling Partner Agentic Primitives & Interfaces at Amazon. Weiling works on Amazon Selling Partner Agentic interfaces and helps partners build solutions that meet their business needs. Hina Vinayak Hina is a Senior Solutions Architect for Selling Partner Agentic Primitives & Interfaces at Amazon. Hina works on Amazon Selling Partner Agentic interfaces and helps build well-architected integrations. Abhinav Mehta Abhinav is a Principal Product Manager – Technical (External Services) at AWS. Abhinav leads the expansion of AWS Quick to different business verticals and partner channels, tailoring it for each kind of customer.

items.title: System 1 决策模型在Feed场景的应用
items.summary: 原创 欢迎关注的 2026-11-19 18:00 北京 决策模型不写文本、只输出概率，在 Feed 推荐中对低活用户和新内容更准；改用 Decoder 架构复用用户缓存后，打分计算量粗略估算降至约四分之一。 。 点击蓝字，关注我们 作者 | Signal 导读 introduction 推荐系统追求既快又准，这正对应《思考，快与慢》里的"快思考"System 1。本文介绍百度 Feed 团队怎样把"只输出概率、不写文本"的决策模型用于推荐打分。这类模型靠语言理解和世界知识判断兴趣，在低活用户和新内容上优势最明显：历史点击最少的一组用户，uAUC 比精排高 2.95%。落地的难点是同一个用户要给约 1800 条候选打分。文章对比了 Encoder、Decoder、双塔三条架构路线，并拆解了缓存复用、知识蒸馏、FP8 量化等降本方法。 全文 5016 字，预计阅读时间 6 分钟 System 1 是心理学家丹尼尔·卡尼曼在《思考，快与慢》中提出的双过程理论里的快速直觉思维模式，又称"快思考"。它恰好映射出我们对推荐系统的期待——既快又准。 TypeSafe AI 于 2026 年 9 月 15 日发布了首个 System One 模型 Jev，核心定位是高速结构化决策：放弃自由文本生成，只输出带类型的概率化结果。它真正的意义在于确立了一种新范式：模型不写文本，只输出概率。 System 1 与 System 2：区别在输出方式 传统大模型偏"慢思考"（System 2），自回归逐词写出一段文本，速度慢，还得二次解析；System 1 模型更接近人的直觉反应，一次前向就把最后的隐状态交给一个小决策头，直接读出带类型的概率，比如点击概率 0.37。 只给概率，带来三点好处： 省掉逐词解码。生成 N 个词要跑 N 次前向，决策模型只跑一次。 概率天然可用于校准。它能和线上其他分数一起排序、融合、过阈值，不必再从文字里抠答案。 自带世界知识。底座是预训练语言模型，这是传统 ID 类特征模型不具备的。 Laya、Kev 等复刻方案里的 pointer head（指针头）同理：通用语言模型要在几万个词里挑一个，指针头只在输入给定的几个选项（如"会点""不会点"）上打分再归一化，既快，也不会答非所问。 GEEK TALK 01 项目「System 1 决策模型」背景 自Jev发布之后，Feed 团队加大了对 System 1 决策模型在 Feed 场景应用的调研。先用官方版本的 laya-multilingual、Jev-API 在 MIND-small 公开数据集与内部场景数据集上做推荐排序打分，初始 AUC 约 0.539，基本等于随机水平；但经过简单微调后 AUC 迅速提升到 0.6 以上，足以证明决策模型能胜任 Feed 打分这一关键角色。随后在实验阶段尝试了多种用户特征组合，并结合若干内容判别力字段微调，快速筛选出一组高价值的上下文特征。首轮线下评估显示，该方案已超越线上粗排基线，在低活用户上更是优于精排 uAUC。 一条样本demo： { "state": { "user": { "recent_queries": [ "某热门行业的岗位待遇怎么样", "该行业适合新人的岗位有哪些", "某岗位最新招聘信息" ], "recent_consumption": [ { "title": "某热播剧集的剧情讨论……", "category": "影视-影视资讯" }, { "title": "某教育话题的热点解读……", "category": "教育-教育资讯" } ] }, "candidate": { "title": "某演员在新剧中的表演评价……", "summary_full": "内容 Agent 产出的候选文章摘要（此处省略）" } }, "questions": { "click": { "type": "bool", "instructions": "结合用户画像、近期阅读兴趣和上下文，该用户会点击这篇候选文章吗？", "criteria": { "true": "会点击", "false": "不会点击" } } } } Laya具备更强的世界知识和推理能力、可有效使用用户和内容理解的产出特征，在新内容/长尾内容/低活用户的预估、 用户和内容的兴趣匹配上存在优势 Case： 一位历史点击较少的低活用户，此前点击过某篇民生政策类内容；系统为其推荐了一篇相关的政策解读后用户点击，决策模型将该内容排进前 5%，而当前系统排序靠后。可见决策模型能基于用户基础属性与少量点击行为，更好地满足个性化需求。 一位对历史与国内时政感兴趣的低活用户，面对一条突发时政内容，决策模型将其排进前 5%，当前系统排序靠后。决策模型具备一定世界知识，在新发布/突发内容上更容易找到目标受众。 越"冷"的用户，收益越大 传统精排依赖大量 ID 类特征和历史统计，用户点击少、内容又新时，就没多少数据可用。决策模型靠语言理解和世界知识，凭少量行为也能推断兴趣，因此在低活用户、新内容和长尾内容上优势最明显。反过来，重度用户点击行为已经很充分，精排本就足够准，决策模型能带来的提升也趋近于零。 GEEK TALK 02 项目目标 为此，我们计划在 Feed 推荐链路层面对 Decision-Model 进行重构，并成立联合优化项目「System 1」，核心目标包括：用更大规模的用户样本探明离线评估的效能极限，同时对在线决策模型进行性能调优，以满足低成本推全的工程要求。 1. 将样本规模扩大至亿级，验证 System 1 决策模型在推荐场景下的 Scaling Law 表现 圈定千万级乃至亿级用户，通过天级任务产出数十亿训练样本，协同多机分布式训练资源，验证"模型/数据/算力越大、效果越好"的缩放规律在推荐场景下是否同样成立，并探明离线评估的效能极限。 2. 通过将决策模型升级为双塔结构，降低在线推理成本，支持高效的线上 A/B 测试与效果验证 提取决策模型的 Last Hidden State 作为向量输出，并将 Item 向量预先缓存至内部存储介质。结合 User 侧的实时预估能力，以低成本完成线上实验的快速验证。 3. 构建标准的 LLM Scoring 架构，通过推理成本优化实现合理成本范围内的全量上线 利用 Decoder 架构完全共享 User 侧 Prefill Cache，将推理成本压至最低，以支持全量部署所需的目标算力规模。 GEEK TALK 03 项目方案 核心难点：user 部分能不能只算一次 Feed 的难点不在模型准不准，而在于同一个用户要对约 1800 条候选打分时，user 部分能不能只算一次。三条架构路线的根本差别，就在于 user 部分能不能缓存、又能缓存到什么程度。 这又取决于注意力能"看"到哪里： Encoder（双向注意力）：每个 token 的表示都依赖左右两侧，后面新增一个 token，前面全部要重算，user 部分几乎无法提前缓存。 Decoder（因果注意力）：前面的 token 看不到后面，它们的 Key / Value 一旦算出就不再变，可以存下来复用，也就是 KV Cache / Prefill Cache。user 在前、候选在后时，user 的 prefill 只算一次，就能被约 1800 条候选共享。 ① 以Laya为代表的纯encoder架构 laya的单次预估延迟极低（tilelang & fp8 & 1k-token单条预估能跑进个位数毫秒内），但是laya-multiligual(mmbert-base模型)天生的双向encoder注意力结构导致在工程上无法提前预计算，而且Feed场景对对链路延迟要求极高 user 编码无法预计算：上下文 state 是 user-nid 信息对，而 mmBERT 是双向编码器，每个 token 的表示都同时依赖左右两侧上下文；一旦后面新增候选 token，前面 user 部分的表示就会随之变化，导致提前计算并缓存 user-state 的收益非常有限。 双向注意力推理算力消耗巨大：受双向注意力结构影响，单卡吞吐有限，在严格的延迟约束（p80速度在数十毫秒）下，处理单个用户一次约 1800 条候选的预估，需要占用相当可观的 GPU 资源。 如上图，线上要对同一个 user 预估约 1800 条候选时，当前架构只能硬算 user-state（约 1k token 上下文中 user 部分占比约 75%），而 mmBERT-base 的 22 层 Transformer 结构让单卡算力相当吃紧。下面是精排预估与 Laya 预估的算力对比。 双向编码器虽有潜力，但这套架构后续的策略迭代空间比较有限。 主要有两点原因： 1、token 数越多，延迟越高。目前对 laya 架构做 32k 上下文 token（约 100KB 的 UTF-8 文本）的测试，单条延迟已接近 1.5s。而策略迭代的方向恰恰是往上加上下文，这块延迟又已经压不动，继续扩展的余地就很小了。 2、蒸馏方面，我们借鉴 tiny-BERT 的多阶段蒸馏：在 teacher 指导下，参数减半的 student 效果损失很小，但小流量仍需不少算力，推全成本会成倍放大。 结合近一周的优化，联合团队综合运用了多项降本手段——FP8 量化（把权重/激活从 16 位压到 8 位，显存减半、张量核心更快）、libtorch（PyTorch 的 C++ 运行时，去掉 Python 调度开销）、tilelang（为特定形状定制高效 GPU 算子）与知识蒸馏——并在线上申请少量 GPU 做真实压测，验证了合适的 batch 与扇出配置可将 P90 耗时控制在 数十ms 以下。最终在满足线上小流量实验标准的前提下，Encoder 路线的小流量成本相比初始版本下降到约三成。 但这依然是一笔巨大的成本开销（评估推全成本约数万张GPU显卡）。 ② 以Qwen为代表的纯decoder架构 既然双向 encoder 的 cache 复用有限，而且同一用户多次 nid 预估的 user-state 基本不变，那么不妨转向 decoder 架构尝试。 如上图， 请求入口一收到用户请求，就向 Decoder 预估集群发送 user 信号，提前触发 user-state 的 prefill 计算。这段计算在全链路上可与「入口开始处理」→「预筛结束」完全并行，可用时间窗口约 数百ms，且 user 只算一次（user-id hash 到同一张卡，保证缓存命中）。 等到预筛结束，再发起约 1800 条候选的预估，此时直接复用已算好的 user-state，只并行计算各候选的增量部分。 粗略统计，encoder 架构换成 decoder 后，在不考虑参数量与网络结构差异的前提下，单个用户批量预估的 1000*1800 tokens 计算量可降低至 750*1+250*1800 tokens（降低至原来的25%）。 更大的空间还是在 decoder。 user-nid state 现在各占 75%:25%，未来的迭代只会让 user 部分明显变大；而在 Feed-decoder 架构下，前面架构图中多出来的 数百ms 正好能把 user-state 提前算好。 效果方面仍有优化空间，decoder 模型选择众多，实际上找到一个（甚至多个）decoder 超越当前 laya 的效果并不难。 所以，我们整个 10 月份的训练工作基本集中在 decoder 架构上；若重点看 uAUC，已经很接近精排了。 目前这套 Decoder 方案已能把小流量的成本控制得相当低，按比例推算推全成本在1万张GPU显卡内。 ③ 以startlux为代表的双塔架构 双塔与交叉编码器的取舍 交叉编码器把 user 与候选拼成一个序列整体编码，两边的每个词都能相互关注，交互充分，但每个 user×item 组合都要整体算一遍。双塔把它拆成独立的 user 塔和 item 塔：item 向量离线算好、小时级更新，线上每个请求只编码一次用户，最后做一步向量匹配。代价是 user 与 item 的细粒度交互会丢失，精度通常不及交叉编码器。它更适合用来低成本验证，再决定是否推全。 借鉴传统的双塔做法，把 startlux-gemma、startlux-decision 0.8B/2B/4B 的交叉编码器（cross-encoder：将 user 与候选拼成一个 prompt，读取 A/B 选项概率）拆成 user 塔和 item 塔，item 向量可以离线算好、小时级更新，线上每个请求只需编码一次用户。这样评估下来，小流量的单次上线成本可降到极低水平。 此外，在线上应用环节，user 预估不一定要实时完成，可视情况调整为次刷更新、小时级更新或天级更新；更新频率越低，成本越低。 三条路线一览 GEEK TALK 04 降本技术全景 推理和训练的成本，大体取决于两件事：算多少，以及每次算多贵。项目的降本手段也围绕这两点展开，可分为四类：复用缓存以减少重复计算、蒸馏裁剪以缩小模型、低精度与算子优化以压低单次开销、LoRA 与前缀打包以节省训练资源。 ① 知识蒸馏：让小模型学会大模型的"判断" 蒸馏的思路是用大模型（teacher）的输出分数来指导小模型（student），让层数更少的 student 也能逼近 teacher 的判断。我们借鉴 tiny-BERT 的多阶段蒸馏，把 mmBERT 的 22 层 encoder 压缩到 11 层。四组对比如下： 具体来看： Accuracy 区分度不够：四组都在 0.91 上下。点击样本占比低时，一律判"不点"也容易判对，所以真正拉开差距的是衡量排序能力的 AUC 和 uAUC。 只裁剪：AUC 0.51、uAUC 0.514，几乎等于随机。层数砍掉又没重新训练，判断力也就丢了。 通用蒸馏：让 student 模仿 teacher 的通用表示，能找回一部分（uAUC 0.569），但对"点不点击"这件具体任务学得不够。 任务蒸馏：直接用 teacher 在本任务上的打分来训练，uAUC 0.652 反超原模型的 0.649，单条耗时也从 20+ms 降到 10+ms。 ② 低精度与工程优化：让每次计算更便宜 FP8 量化：把权重和激活从 16 位浮点压到 8 位浮点，显存占用约减半，GPU 的张量核心处理 8 位数据也更快。 libtorch：PyTorch 的 C++ 运行时，去掉 Python 层的调度开销，适合延迟敏感的在线服务。 tilelang：用来写 GPU 算子的编程语言，能为特定形状定制高效算子。Laya 靠它 + fp8，把 1k token 的单条预估压进个位数毫秒。 batch 与扇出调优：在线申请少量 GPU 做真实压测，验证 batch=20、单次扇出约 90 次时 P90 耗时可控制在 数十ms 以下；在小流量实验标准下，Encoder 路线成本相比初始版本下降到约三成。 ③ LoRA 与冻结层：让训练装得下、跑得起 全量微调要更新所有参数，显存和耗时都很大。LoRA 的做法是冻结原权重 W，只训练一对小矩阵 A、B，让更新量 ΔW = B·A，其中 r 是"秩"（这里取 16），r 越小，要训练的参数越少。再叠加冻结底部若干层，只训练上层，进一步省显存。 可以看出：冻结一半层更省资源，代价是 uAUC 下降约 0.0064。 ④ 共享前缀打包：训练时也复用 user 部分 同一个用户会对应很多候选，样本里 user 前缀完全相同。共享前缀打包可以理解为：把共享同一 user 前缀的多条样本放进同一个序列里，前缀只算一次，每条候选只补自己那一段。这和线上"user prefill 只算一次"是同一个思想——训练端是打包，推理端是缓存。 GEEK TALK 05 项目成果 Encoder 模型（laya）优化 联合团队采用 libtorch、FP8、蒸馏等多种手段，小流量成本相比初始版本下降到约三成。 Decoder 模型（qwen 系）优化 联合团队通过复用 user-cache 等多种手段，进一步大幅降低小流量成本，相比Encoder模型下降到约三成。 双塔模型（startlux）进展 决策-双塔模型架构充分利用提前缓存的优势，继续降低实验成本。 END 推荐阅读 从代码生成到需求交付：DarkFactory 的工程实践 研发Loop的上下文优化与多Agent协作实践 AI 内容核查怎么做：智能内容 AI 核查系统实践 QCon上海2026：百度 items.title: 阿里巴巴两篇论文获 ATC 2026 最佳论文奖，并在港研讨 AI Native 系统的可靠性与效率
items.summary: 原创 阿里技术 2026-11-19 20:02 浙江 11 月 15 日，在 ATC 2026 期间，阿里巴巴于香港沙田万怡酒店举办 Alibaba Hong Kong Forum，主题为「面向下一代人工智能的全栈协同设计」（Full-Stack Co-Design for Next-Generation AI: Infrastructure, Systems, Models and Data）。设 AI Infra & AI Systems、Model & Data 两个并行 Session，高校学者与阿里巴巴技术专家分别介绍研究进展与当前面临的技术难题，30+ 位高校学者、50+ 位高校学生和阿里技术专家参与了本次技术交流。 11 月 16 日，大会公布最佳论文奖：本届 ATC 录用 135 篇论文，阿里巴巴入选 12 篇（文末附 12 篇论文解读链接🔗），并在 6 篇最佳论文中占 2 篇。 01 最佳论文：从生产系统里「长」出来的问题 本次阿里巴巴集团获评的两篇最佳论文分别为《Model-as-a-Service in the Wild: Characterizing Production LLM Inference Clusters at Scale》和《Lean: Saving OSS Network Cost by Application-Infrastructure Coordination》。 最佳论文《Model-as-a-Service in the Wild》获奖团队合影 平台技术团队的获奖论文《Model-as-a-Service in the Wild: Characterizing Production LLM Inference Clusters at Scale》，依托十万卡级大模型服务平台 xMaaS，研究连续六个月、覆盖约 30 万个应用与 7 万个模型变体的真实运行数据，从集群、应用与模型三个层面揭示显存预留与实际使用不匹配、冷模型长期占用资源等问题，为异构算力调度、精细化显存管理与弹性扩缩容提供生产依据，并同步开放脱敏数据。工作由平台技术团队与香港中文大学（深圳）余旻晨老师团队合作完成。 最佳论文《Lean》获奖团队合影 阿里云团队的获奖论文《Lean: Saving OSS Network Cost by Application-Infrastructure Coordination》聚焦对象存储 OSS 的网络成本，以应用与网络基础设施协同设计为思路，用 SRv6 实现轻量化边缘接入、灵活流量调度与业务流量物理隔离。系统已在生产环境持续运行四年，同等生产流量下将 OSS 网络总成本较原方案降低 55.6%。工作由阿里云与上海交通大学徐尔茨老师合作完成，徐尔茨同时担任本次系统 Room 主持人。两篇论文都以生产系统的真实约束为起点，再把结论放回生产验证。 02 两个研讨 Room：全栈协同设计为何成为共同议题 本次 Alibaba Hong Kong Forum 分设系统和模型两个 Room 进行研讨。主题设置上，系统方向讨论训推软硬协同与 Agent Infra 的可靠性，由上海交通大学徐尔茨主持；模型方向讨论 LLM 与多模态训练推理、Agentic RL、视频生成与数据评测，并要求模型侧反向定义系统所需的数据、实时性与安全边界，由香港科技大学王威主持。 2.1 系统 Room：从推理调度到 Agent 运行时的问题链 系统 Room 由来自阿里巴巴集团的谷朴开场，他表示，AI Infra 是一个非常巨大的机会，算力基建正以前所未有的速度扩张，很多天花板的突破需要从新的架构、新的方法，端到端、全栈地重新设计，才有机会把效率发挥到最大。 谷朴｜阿里巴巴集团｜系统 Room 开场 随后，四位来自阿里巴巴的技术专家依次展开 MaaS 资源调度与资源管理、推理引擎、Agentic OS，以及万亿参数与长序列模型的分布式训练。 推理服务：调度的前提已经改变 岩泉把大模型推理对基础设施的改变归到一句话，那就是：调度不再是把请求分给空闲机器，而要在有状态、强 SLO、负载还不可预测三个约束同时成立的前提下做决定。他给的两个例子最能说明这件事有多「新」——冷扩容实例因为没缓存预热要扛 100% 的计算，而热实例只扛 5%，弹性增益天然要打折；而模型与卡型的匹配决策周期，已经从搜推广时代的半年一年被压到了周级别。当 MaaS 推理、快训练、AIGC 训练和 Agent workflow 这些全都带状态的负载必须混在同一个集群里，资源调度就不再是单点优化问题，而是调度、网络和存储要一起重新设计的 co-design 问题。 喜德指出，真实 MaaS 流量下的多卡、多节点推理，计算、通信与显存成本相互牵制。团队已具备缓存感知路由、分层 KV 与 TP／PP／EP／DP 等方法，并在探索 EPLB、DP Balance、动态投机与 Kernel 优化。他提出的合作方向是联合成本模型与系统原型，在同负载、同硬件、同 SLO 条件下对照验证 Goodput、单位成本与资源开销。 训练系统：效率与正确性一起验证 雾汀结合生产案例，分享了万亿参数、百万 token 上下文训练面临的挑战。通过前置健康检查、分层 Checkpoint 和流水线预热，案例中的有效训练时间占比从约 90.5% 提升至 97%。 团队介绍了与高校合作的 VRouter、Tessera 和 Libra，分别应对 MoE 负载不均、通信开销和长序列训练扩展问题。Libra 在百万 token 上下文实验中，将数据并行扩展效率从 27.6% 提升至 70.3%。雾汀还以梯度求和为例，说明在低精度计算中，同一组数仅仅改变累加顺序，就可能得到不同的结果，进而影响模型参数更新。 Agent 运行时：系统软件的职责边界 伯瑜的问题位于系统软件层面。Agent 调用工具、修改环境并等待结果，任务进度分散在上下文、文件与远端服务之中，多个 Agent 还共享文件、工具与执行资源。开源系统软件 ANOLISA 已支撑阿里云 AgenticOS 对外服务，集成任务管理、安全治理、信息处理与恢复能力。他希望资源管理面向完整任务，协调跨轮次、跨 Agent 的状态，形成能够表达资源、权限与动作效果的公共系统接口。 学界观点：沿同一条链的不同切入点 六位学者沿着同一条链路发表观点：陈全与须成忠处理资源与调度，黄嘉逸与吴川处理训练与后训练，吴明瑜处理运行时正确性，潘恬落到网络底座。 陈全｜上海交通大学计算机学院先进计算研究所教授 陈全从 Agent 长会话切入：KV 与状态长期驻留显存，休眠会话持续占用资源，沙箱需兼顾秒级启动、高密度与强隔离。他将预填充与解码逻辑分离、物理混部，按 Transformer 层切分实现 SM 空分复用，优先保障解码阶段的每 token 时延，其余算力分配给预填充；沙箱镜像的只读页直接映射共享、写入私有，checkpoint 原位封存为新的只读来源；KV 卸载要求缓存池不打断 CUDA Graph、预取无损。 须成忠｜澳门大学讲座教授、科技学院院长 须成忠将分散在各卡的 HBM 视为统一 KV 池，主张将计算调度到数据所在位置。工具处理占据 Agent 时延的主要部分，CPU 的角色由辅助转为命令层，因此可选择性地将部分解码注意力卸载至 CPU，并在云边之间动态移动流水线边界。其中 Axon 采用阿里 Aone 的生产 trace 做回放评测，也是阿里入选 ATC 2026 的十二篇之一，构成当天学界与业务最直接的接口。 黄嘉逸｜香港科技大学（广州）功能枢纽微电子学域助理教授 黄嘉逸关注 MoE 的通信与负载。All-to-All 与专家计算存在强数据依赖，难以重叠；推理阶段热门专家的负载可达平均值的数倍。ScMoE（ICML 2025）以 shortcut 连接使 MoE 层不依赖上一层的中间表达，从而实现通信与计算的重叠。推理侧以扩展的本地专家选择配合 token drop，用闲置算力换取精度，或采用张量级与神经元级双稀疏，在精度与效率之间取得更优的折中。 吴川｜香港大学计算机科学系教授、IEEE Fellow 吴川的报告聚焦后训练框架。RL 的采样、训练、验证与奖励模块相互阻塞，长尾轨迹导致 GPU 空闲，失败经验也难以跨轮次复用。veRL／HybridFlow（EuroSys 2025）将算法写为单控制器、计算交由多控制器，先实现模块解耦；Laminar （EuroSys 2026）进一步做轨迹级异步采样与按完成量动态重打包，将生成与训练解耦；下一步是将新鲜、回放与过期数据混合纳入经验缓冲，走向以经验与验证驱动的 RSI。 吴明瑜｜上海交通大学计算机学院副研究员（IPADS） 吴明瑜讨论多个 Agent 同时修改一套运行中系统的情形。K8s 配置、共享文档等持续变化的状态会出现写偏斜，即各 Agent 单独执行均正确、并发执行后整体结果错误。经典并发控制将任务视为黑盒，冲突时整体阻塞或重新执行，但 Agent 的读集远大于实际使用的集合，任务按分钟与真实 token 计价，重新执行代价高昂。他以运行时记录的读写与输出构建细粒度因果图，冲突时通知 Agent 自行分析因果、仅修复受影响的步骤，并配合补偿与多版本读，最后配套 agent 工作流自动给工具绑定读写集与补偿动作。 潘恬指出，云网络的一些传统假设在 AI 负载下需要修正：拥塞瓶颈由网络部分转移至端侧接收，主机内PCIe 余量被压缩、PFC 背压向网络扩散；连接不再独立表示业务，RDMA 控制面使用 TCP建连、数据面使用 UDP传输，经过负载均衡器时需跨连接关联；访问服务地址到 Agent 运行时才确定，无法直接携带在数据包头；端点网络接入因 Sandbox 生命周期短而需要频繁配置更新。相应的探索包括事件驱动的最后一跳裁剪、支持 RDMA 穿越负载均衡、以 vNIC 预热池缩短网络准备时间。MCP Gateway 在注册时建立语义与词法双索引，在线融合检索候选工具，实现LLM context压缩和工具精确检索；这项工作也在阿里入选的十二篇之列。 系统侧的链条由此闭合。资源与调度、训练与后训练、运行时正确性、网络底座，共同要求是结论能在同负载、同硬件、同 SLO 下复现。 2.2 模型 Room：数据、评测与生成如何反向定义系统 模型 Room 由阿里巴巴集团的喜德进行开场。他说道，当天分享的都是商业化场景中面临的真实问题，希望和学界一起寻求更好的解法，把这些关键问题讨论清楚就是最大的收获。 喜德｜阿里巴巴集团｜模型 Room 开场 喜德介绍了四位阿里技术专家的分享方向：多模态生成场景下的训练与推理 Infra、面向真实业务的大模型评测、长程 Agent 的自我演化，以及支撑 Agent 运行的 Harness 工程。 生成模型 Infra：训练效率决定能力上限，部署效率决定成本 家忙认为，现有工程体系尚不足以承载参数量与数据量增长带来的效果收益。训练侧采用 packing 与动态并行、专家均衡与 FP8；后训练作业的多任务、多租户特性通过优先级、公平性与碎片整理进行调度；推理侧将量化、稀疏、蒸馏与 Cache 联合使用，并对有损优化做在线效果监控与自适应回退。他向学界提出的问题是预训练效率翻倍的机会点、视频生成与世界模型的每秒成本还需要哪些突破，以及如何高效判断有损优化是否满足效果需求。 评测与 Harness：结果可信性的建立 雄道介绍面向真实业务的大模型评测，出发点是基准本身未必可信：公开基准数量众多，被主流引用的高质量很少，开源评测集普遍存在错题与数据污染现象。团队先确立评测集健康度指数 BHI 作为基准选择准则；评测对象从单轮答题扩展到真实职业任务，并将模型与 Harness 放在一起评估——同一模型更换一套 Harness，分数即发生变化。判分采用动态评分细则逐维加权，同时对过程建模。他列出的未解决问题包括长程多轮的过程判分、真实任务如何数据化、出题到质控的全链路自动化，以及专家偏好如何放大为稳定标准并量化一致性。 懿川进一步介绍 Harness 工程的实践和 RSI 设计。随着模型的能力不断提升，对于模型能力的要求也从“让模型回答正确”转向“让系统可靠完成任务”。在 Harness 工程上拆分为规划、路由、工具接口、执行与验证几层，同时采用统一轨迹格式与适配层把 M×N 的模型—环境适配降为 M+N。通过将 Harness 进行设计优化，设计 api proxy 的方案记录 token 与 logprobs，并持续迭代 Harness 能力，进一步实现 Harness 能力内化到模型，从而实现 Harness 和模型的协同演进。 长程 Agent：让模型反过来优化系统 长程 Agent 把这条链路接回系统侧。垂瑟指出，状态依赖、误差累积与延迟反馈使单步正确不等于任务完成。他以 Engineering 任务作为长程 RL 环境，将编译检查、数值回归、性能测量与 EDA 验证转化为 dense reward，让模型通过中间反馈持续探索、诊断与修正。已完成的实验中，Qwen 在 Kernel 优化、推理系统适配与芯片设计中持续迭代数十小时，完成从算子提速、端到端性能优化到规格驱动的 RTL、验证与物理实现。被优化的对象，正是系统 Room 讨论的推理系统与芯片实现。 学界观点：数据、机制、算法与生成 本场的五位学者分别回答上游的问题：评测是否可信，数据从哪里来，信号是否可靠，学习算法能否持续，生成结果能否可控。 王历伟｜香港中文大学助理教授、LaVi Lab 负责人 王历伟的分享主题是《大语言模型的测评与进化》，与雄道形成学界与业务两侧的对照，工作沿“测评—进化”两条线展开。测评侧，他于 2023 年推出首批综合性中文大模型评测平台 CLEVA，覆盖 31 项任务、84 个数据集、37 万条测试样本与 9 个评测维度。值得一提的是，该平台已被斯坦福 HELM 收录，在其 2025 年综述中是唯一专注于中文评测的榜单。 针对基准污染，他提出 C²LEVA 以被动防御与主动防御相结合自动生成全新试题——爬虫与模拟器采集语料、入库后经预处理、污染检测与数据增广再释放为数据集，在中英文 22 项任务上测试了 15 个模型；并将动态评测扩展到视频，NeMoBench 在 13,486 段视频上自动生成 31,378 个时序定位问题。 进化侧，他提出基于反馈的测试时训练（FTTT）：由验证器判定答案对错，再用一个学习到的优化器依据失败尝试的梯度预测下一次权重更新，使模型不依赖一次性的静态训练，在推理阶段即可从反馈中持续改进。 骆昱宇｜香港科技大学（广州）助理教授、DIAL Lab 负责人 骆昱宇关注训练数据的来源与筛选。Agent 训练需要可交互、可验证、可复现的轨迹，以有限状态机合成网页环境，批量生成轨迹；数据选择不再额外执行一次推理，而是复用训练前向的副产物——loss、梯度、logits 与 attention——在样本与 token 两层筛选。推理侧将专家拆分为原子专家、以笛卡尔路由降低开销，目标是把执行瓶颈从访存受限转向计算受限。 邹荻凡｜香港大学助理教授 邹荻凡的报告系统性梳理了 LLM 可解释性的多个层次。理论层面，报告从 Transformer 的表达力、训练动力学与泛化出发，讨论上下文学习、思维链与推理能力的数学基础，并进一步揭示模型能力与网络深度及内部计算机制之间的关系。现象与物理驱动层面，报告强调通过可控数据干预、因果中介分析和机制观测，刻画模型真实决策依据，以及训练与规模变化对模型能力的影响。通用解释工具层面，报告以 circuits 与稀疏自编码器 SAE 为代表，覆盖机制定位、模型编辑、控制与扩散语言模型等应用，并指出目前常用的可解释工具 SAE 在 token 级容易停留在表层特征，chunk 级更有利于发现可靠语义特征。更进一步，报告还尝试从第一性原理出发，设计更自然可解释、更节能的模型架构。同时，报告阐述了可解释性研究对生产环境中性能的作用与机制，并强调其应反哺算法与数据设计，形成理解机制、验证效用、改进模型的闭环。 潘玲｜香港科技大学助理教授、智能决策实验室负责人 潘玲以“Keep RL learning at scale”为主线，回顾了强化学习从经典 RL、深度 RL 到基础模型RL的几次发展浪潮。在适应性上，她指出 RL 面临非平稳的学习环境，智能体会逐渐丧失学习可塑性；她提出以梯度幅值而非激活值度量神经元活性，周期性重置休眠神经元，并以动态拓扑生长调和稳定性与塑性的两难；提出在 SFT 到 RL 的交接处恢复模型塑性。在实用性上，她指出大模型可验证奖励的决策 MDP 结构比传统控制问题的 MDP 具备更清晰的结构，算法因而可以大幅简化：评估均匀随机策略、再根据其 Q 值贪心行动即接近最优，极简RL算法在多个模型规模与分布外任务上超过大模型RL算法；对图像与视频生成等不可验证奖励，则以多样性寻求抑制 reward hacking。最后，她展望了让 RL 在规模化中持续学习的路线：配合算法与系统协同设计，构建可靠的 RL 技术栈。 陈启峰｜香港科技大学副教授、CAiRE 主任 陈启峰的报告聚焦可控视频生成。可执行的世界已能给出相机、运动与持久状态的控制，但通用视频渲染器在事件时序、未见视角与回访时的外观一致性上仍不稳定。他的路线是 code-to-real：Builder 与 Reviewer 构建世界，Planner 与 Compiler 产出代理与状态轨迹，再以"生成—审核—修复"的有预算循环产出合格配对，最后冻结主干、每个世界一个 LoRA 适配器做递归蒸馏。其分工是程序保存世界状态，渲染器学习如何呈现。 2.3 开放问题与现场讨论 报告之外，为加强学界和业界的交流，本次 Alibaba Hong Kong Forum 设置了研讨环节。 系统 Room 从云端与本地 Agent 的系统支撑问起。阿里云技术专家认为两边并存，需要同一层面向 Agent 的系统抽象；云上更像沙箱，本地握着用户数据，操作须更谨慎。Agent 大部分时间在等待，难点是系统不了解任务状态，挂起与恢复要快到用户察觉不到。安全被反复提起：本地权限放开后环境可能被篡改，可信执行环境是一个思路。 模型 Room 两组讨论评测、数据与奖励的可信性。可解释性与数据组认为，判断“某个激活对应什么概念”仍靠假设与对比实验，没有理论保证；垂类与通用数据的投入与配比未定。视觉生成组先谈“训不动”：视频 token 极长，几十秒时长前后难一致；“高质量”标准互相冲突，审美难量化，多模态 RL 的 reward 难定义也易被 hack。与会者倾向从特定场景的小规模数据构建与验证开始合作。两组其实是同一问题：评测、数据与奖励都需要可信裁判。 03 Alibaba Hong Kong Night × AliStar Wonder Night晚宴 当晚，Alibaba Hong Kong Night × AliStar Wonder Night 晚宴圆满举办。晚宴进一步汇聚了 30+ 位高校学者、百余位学生，与阿里巴巴业务技术团队展开面对面交流，为高校师生与业务专家提供了开放、平等的对话平台。 现场特设的论文 Poster 展示区前，同学们与业务技术专家就具体的研究方向进行了深入探讨。在自由交流环节，与会师生不仅更直观地了解了阿里巴巴的前沿技术探索与产业落地中的真实难题，也让阿里业务团队听到了来自高校的研究思路与观察。期间，阿里星 HR 团队与青年学者们就课题方向及职业发展规划进行了深度沟通。 阿里巴巴希望通过此类交流，推动更多师生围绕产业问题开展研究，为后续科研合作、学生实习和人才交流建立长效联系。目前，“阿里星顶尖人才计划”持续面向全球开放招募，我们期待与更多顶尖大脑并肩同行，在真实的产业场景中，将研究落地为改变世界的力量。 04 展望 接下来，阿里巴巴会把更多生产一线的真实问题带进高校实验室，学界的新方法也会放到阿里的真实负载里检验，双方在 AI 系统和模型研究上能做成的事，会比今天更多。 现场花絮： *延伸阅读：阿里巴巴 12 篇论文入选全球系统顶会 ATC 2026（内附下载） 欢迎留言一起参与讨论~ 跳转微信打开
